div.p: . . . except that, if men report to the king any who are behaving disorderly, those are punished at once; but over those who do not draw near to the gods there is set the appointed tribe of evil spirits, by whom many of the godless are driven frantic and are persuaded to court death, in the belief that they will fly up to heaven when they have torn their souls violently from the body. And there are some, too, who pursue the deserts instead of the cities, though man is by nature a social and civilised animal; they have been given over to evil spirits, by whom they are led into this hatred of mankind. Many of them have even devised for themselves chains and collars: so on every side does the evil spirit drive them, to which they have willingly surrendered themselves, having revolted from the everlasting and saving gods. But concerning these men it is enough to have said so much; I shall now return to the point from which I digressed.
To Eustathius

I, on receiving your letter, at once sent Archelaus, giving him letters to carry to you, and the warrant, as you bade, for a longer time. As for your wish to view the Ocean, you shall have everything according to your desire, God willing, if only you take care to guard against the boorishness of the Gauls and against the winter. But this shall be as is pleasing to God; and I swear to you, by him who is to me the author of all good things and my saviour, that I pray to live for this reason, that I may be of some use to you. And when I say "to you," I mean the true philosophers; and you, being persuaded that you are one of these, know how I loved you and love you and pray to see you. May divine providence keep you in good health for many years, most longed-for and most beloved brother. I send my greetings to the holy Hippia and to your children.

As for the practice of justice according to the civil laws, it is plain that the governors of the cities will see to it; but it would be fitting that you too should exhort men not to transgress those laws, since they are sacred to the gods. And since the priestly life ought to be more venerable than the political, men must be led toward it and instructed; and the better sort, in all likelihood, will follow. For my own part I pray that they may all do so, but I hope it of those who are by nature reasonable and earnest, since they will recognise that these teachings are properly their own.
To Priscus

As to your goodness coming to me, if indeed you intend it, take counsel now with the gods and be eager; for perhaps a little later not even I shall have leisure. Seek out for me all the works of Iamblichus on his namesake; you alone are able, for your sister's son-in-law has copies that are in good order. And, if I am not mistaken, a marvellous sign occurred to me at the very moment I was writing this part. I beseech you, do not let the followers of Theodorus din it even into your ears that the divine Iamblichus was truly ambitious, and the third after Pythagoras and Plato; and if it is bold of me to make my own mind plain to you, since it follows those who are inspired, the pardon is not unreasonable. For you yourself are mad about Iamblichus in philosophy, and about his namesake in theosophy. And I think the rest, as Apollodorus says, are nothing compared with these men. As to the collections of Aristotle which you made, I say only this much to you: you have made me a pupil falsely inscribed as yours; for Maximus of Tyre could initiate me but a little into Platonic logic in six books, but you, by means of a single book, made me, perhaps, a very Bacchant of the Aristotelian philosophy, or at least a bearer of the thyrsus. And if I speak the truth, when you come to me you will find many proofs of it among my works of last winter.
Concerning that abominable creature of doubtful sex, I should gladly learn this: when did he speak these things about me, before he met me or after? Make plain to me, then, whatever you are able.

But you see that I have passed over many great things. It is most worth your while to learn how all at once we perceived the manifestation of the gods, and in what manner we escaped so great a multitude of plotters, having slain no one, taken away no one's money, and only put under guard those whom we caught in the very act. These things, perhaps, ought not to be written but spoken; yet I think you will be very glad to hear them. We worship the gods openly, and the greater part of the army that came down with me is god-fearing. We sacrifice oxen in public. We have rendered to the gods many hecatombs as thank-offerings. The gods bid me restore their worship in all its purity, so far as I can, and I obey them, and that gladly; for they say they will give great rewards for our labours, if we are not slothful. Evagrius has come to me . . . of the god honoured among us. . . .

There is a shrine of Hector, where a bronze statue stands in a small chapel. Over against this they set up the great Achilles, in the open air. If you have seen the place, you doubtless recognise what I mean. The story, then, on account of which the great Achilles, set over against him, has taken up the whole open space, you may hear from the guides. But I, finding the altars still burning, I might almost say still bright, and the image of Hector glistening with oil, looked at Pegasius and said: "What is this? Do the people of Ilion sacrifice?"—putting him gently to the test, to see how he was minded. And he said: "And what is strange in this, that they should worship a good man, their own fellow-citizen, as we worship the martyrs?" Now the comparison was not sound; but his disposition, examined in the circumstances of those times, was honourable. What followed next? "Let us go," I said, "to the precinct of Ilian Athena." And he very eagerly led me there, and opened the temple, and, as though calling me to witness, showed me all the statues perfectly preserved; and he did none of those things which those impious men are wont to do, sketching the memorial on their impious foreheads; nor did he hiss, as they do, to himself. For the height of their theology consists in these two things: to hiss at the daemons and to draw the cross upon their foreheads.

What, then, is this which I say I now entrust to you? To rule over all the temples throughout Asia, choosing the priests in each city and assigning to each what befits him. Now there befits a ruler, first, fairness, and after it kindness, and love of man toward those who deserve to obtain such treatment. For whoever wrongs men, and is unholy toward the gods, and insolent toward all, must either be taught with frankness or chastened with severity. As to all that must be ordained in common concerning all the priests more fully, you shall presently learn it with the rest; but for the present I wish to suggest a few things to you. And it is just that you should obey me in such matters. For I do not, as all the gods know, improvise most such things; rather, if any man does, I am cautious and avoid innovation, in all things, one might say, but especially in things concerning the gods, holding that we ought to keep the ancestral laws which were given from the beginning. That the gods gave them is plain; for they would not have been so good had they come simply from men. But since it has come about that they have been neglected and corrupted, wealth and luxury having prevailed, I think we ought to attend to such matters as from the very hearth. Seeing, then, that there is much carelessness among us toward the gods, and that all reverence toward the higher powers has been driven out by impure and vulgar luxury, I have always lamented these things in private. For those who give heed to the discipline of Jewish piety are so fervent that they choose death for its sake, and endure every want and famine, that they may not taste swine's flesh, nor what is strangled, nor what has been throttled; while we are so slack in things concerning the gods that we have forgotten the things of our fathers, and no longer even know whether any such thing was ever ordained. But these Jews, being in part god-fearing, since they worship a god who is truly most powerful and most good, who governs the world of sense, whom, I well know, we too worship under other names, seem to me to do what is reasonable in not transgressing their laws; in this only do they err, that, while they please this god above all, they do not worship the other gods also, but think them allotted to us, the nations, alone, raised to this folly by a barbaric arrogance. But those of the Galilaean impiety, as though it were some disease, their own . . .

Compare, then, this letter of mine with the one I sent you a little while ago, and mark the difference. How many praises of you did I write then? But now, by the gods, though I wish to praise you, I cannot, because of your lawlessness. A people dares, like dogs, to tear a man to pieces, and then is not ashamed to lift up to the gods hands dripping with blood. But Georgius deserved to suffer such things. Yes, and I might say he deserved worse and bitterer than these. And on your account, you will say. I agree to this myself; but if you say it was at your hands, this I no longer grant. For you have laws, which ought to be honoured and cherished above all by every man in private. Yet, since it happens that some individuals transgress, still the public order at least must be well-governed, and you must obey the laws and not transgress the ordinances which from the beginning were well established. It has been a piece of good fortune for you, men of Alexandria, that you committed such a transgression in my reign, who, out of reverence for the god, and for the sake of my uncle and namesake, who ruled over Egypt itself and over your city, preserve toward you a brotherly goodwill. For a power that will not be despised, and the sterner and purer rule, would never overlook the daring of a people without purging it, like a grievous disease, with a bitter medicine. But I, for the reasons I have just named, apply to you the gentlest remedy: admonition and words, by which I well know you will be the more persuaded, if indeed you are, as I hear, of old time Hellenes, and if even now there remains in you, in mind and pursuits, some worthy and noble stamp of that nobility.

Visit the governors rarely at their houses, but write to them for the most part. And when they enter the city, let no priest go out to meet them, but only, when they go to the temples of the gods, within the porches. Let no soldier lead the way before them within, but whoever wishes may follow; for the moment a man comes to the threshold of the precinct he has become a private person. For you yourself rule, as you know, over those within, since the divine ordinance requires this. And those who obey are in truth god-fearing, while those who cling to their pride are vainglorious and empty of true honour.

In this I have perhaps chattered and prated to you, having suffered something foolish; for I have praised myself like Astydamas. But that I might persuade you that your presence, as that of a sensible man, will be of more use to us than it will take anything from your leisure, I have written this. Hasten, then, as I said, using the public post; and having stayed with us as long as is dear to you, you shall go wherever you wish, sent on by us, as is fitting.

But now the Corinthians—for so it is more decent to put it: that the city is reckoned as belonging to them—being puffed up to ill-doing by the imperial city, compel her to contribute to them, and they began, as they say, this innovation seven years ago, having no respect for the immunity of the Delphians or the Eleans, which was granted to them for holding the sacred games among them. For of the four greatest and most splendid contests in Hellas, as we know, the Eleans hold the Olympic games, the Delphians the Pythian, the Corinthians the games at the Isthmus, and the Argives celebrate the festival of the Nemean games. How then is it reasonable that those should keep the immunity granted of old, while these, who were freed long ago from like expenses, and perhaps not even subjected at the first, should now be robbed of the privilege they were granted? Besides, the Eleans and Delphians are wont to hold their famous quadrennial festival but once; whereas the Nemean games are held twice among the Argives, as the Isthmian among the Corinthians. And in this same period two other contests of the same kind are now also set before the Argives, so that there are four in all in four years. How then is it reasonable that those others should be untroubled, performing their service once, while these are subjected besides to the contributions of others, on top of fourfold services at home, and these too not even for a Hellenic and ancient festival? For it is not for the equipment of gymnastic or musical contests that the Corinthians need their great expenditures, but for the hunting-shows that are often held in the theatres they buy bears and panthers. And they, indeed, naturally bear the greatness of the outlay because of their wealth, especially as many cities, in all likelihood, join with them in this, so that they purchase the pleasure of their pride. But the Argives, who are poorer in money, and who are forced to be laid under contribution for a foreign spectacle and for the benefit of others, how shall they not suffer things unjust and unlawful and unworthy of the ancient power and renown of the city, being neighbours of those Corinthians whom it were rather fitting that they should love, if it be rightly said that "not even an ox would perish, but for the wickedness of a neighbour"? The Argives, it seems, accuse the Corinthians of meddling not over one little ox, but over many great expenses, for which they are not justly accountable.

As to the matters about which you wrote me, I approve everything, I admire all that you have in mind; nothing in those plans is to be rejected. Know, therefore, that I will also do everything, the gods aiding.

I received, however, the gifts—a silver bowl weighing one mina, and a piece of gold coin. I wished to summon you to me, as you wrote. But already the spring is showing itself, and the trees are budding, and the swallows, all but expected, when they come in, drive us, their fellow-soldiers, from the houses, and say that we must keep beyond the borders. We shall march through your country, so that, the gods willing, I may better meet with you among your own people. And this, I think, will be soon, unless some divine hindrance arise; and even this we pray the gods to avert.

The multitudes, then, deceived by those who are called clergy, are plainly stirred up to faction now that this license is taken away. For those who have tyrannised over them are not content that they are not punished for the evils they have done, but, longing for their former dominion, because they are no longer suffered to sit as judges and write wills and appropriate the inheritances of others and assign everything to themselves, they pull every rope of disorder, and, as the saying is, pour fire upon fire, and dare to add greater evils to their former ones, leading the multitudes into discord. It has seemed good to me, therefore, to proclaim to all the peoples by this edict, and to make plain, that they should not join in faction with the clergy, nor be persuaded by them to take up stones, nor disobey the magistrates; but let them assemble as much as they will, and pray such prayers as they think fit for themselves; but if the clergy persuade them to raise faction on their own behalf, let them no longer consent, lest they pay the penalty.

I am very much ashamed, by the gods, men of Alexandria, that any Alexandrian at all confesses himself a Galilaean. The fathers of the true Hebrews were once slaves to the Egyptians; but now you, men of Alexandria, who have conquered the Egyptians—for your founder conquered Egypt—submit to a voluntary slavery to those who have despised the doctrines of their fathers, directly against the ancient ordinances. And there comes into you no memory of that old felicity, when there was fellowship with the gods for all Egypt, and we enjoyed many good things. But those who now have brought in this new preaching among you, of what good have they been authors to the city? Tell me. Your founder was a god-fearing man, Alexander the Macedonian, in no way, by Zeus, after the manner of any of these, nor after that of all the Hebrews, who were far surpassed by them. Why, even the Ptolemy son of Lagus was better than they; and Alexander, had he entered into rivalry with the Romans, would have given them a hard struggle. What then of the Ptolemies after the founder, who reared your city like a true-born daughter? It was not by the words of Jesus that they increased her, nor by the teaching of the Galilaeans, most hateful to the gods, that they wrought for her this good ordering by which she is now prosperous. Third, since we Romans became masters of her, having taken her from the Ptolemies who ruled ill, Augustus, visiting your city and conversing with your citizens, said: "Men of Alexandria, I release the city from all blame, out of reverence for the great god Sarapis, and for the sake of the people themselves and the greatness of the city; and a third cause of my goodwill toward you is my friend Arius." Now this Arius was a citizen of yours, and a companion of Caesar Augustus, a philosopher.

But on your own account these things have been said by me, more than enough; only it is perhaps necessary, because of you, to defend myself before the others, that I rashly called you to a partnership in affairs. This I was not the first nor the only one to suffer, O Dionysius. Your namesake deceived even the great Plato; and so did the Athenian Callippus. For he says that he knew him to be wicked, but that he would never have hoped for so great a magnitude of evil in him. And what need to speak of these things, when even Hippocrates, the best of the sons of Asclepius, said: "The sutures in the head deceived my judgement"? If, then, those men were deceived in matters they knew, and the rule of his art escaped the physician, is it strange if Julian, hearing that Nilus Dionysius had suddenly turned brave, was deceived? You hear of that Phaedo of Elis, and you know the story; or, if you are ignorant, inquire more carefully; but I, at any rate, will say this. He thought that nothing is incurable by philosophy, and that all men are cleansed by her of all manner of lives, pursuits, desires—absolutely all such things. For if she availed only with those well-born and well-bred, there would be nothing wonderful in her work; but if she leads even those so disposed up to the light, she seems to me to be marvellous beyond measure. From these considerations my judgement about you inclined, little by little, to the better—the gods all know it. So I ranked your case neither among the first nor among the second of the best men. You yourself, perhaps, know it; or, if you are ignorant, ask the noble Symmachus. For I am persuaded that he would never willingly lie, being by nature truthful in all things. But if you are vexed that I did not honour you above all, I blame myself for ranking you even among the last, and I am grateful to all the gods and goddesses who hindered you from sharing in affairs and becoming our friend. . . . For even if the poets say much of Rumour, that she is a goddess, and let her be, if you will, at least a daemon, this Rumour, we must not give too much heed to her, since the daemonic is by nature not wholly pure nor perfectly good, like the race of the gods, but partakes somehow of the other side too. But if of the other daemons it is not lawful to say this, of Rumour I know, when I say that she reports much falsely, and much truly, I should never be convicted of false witness.

I read the discourse yesterday, almost before my morning meal; and having taken my meal, before I rested, I gave back the rest of my reading. Happy are you who can so speak, or rather so think. O the eloquence, O the wit, O the understanding, O the division, O the arguments, O the arrangement, O the openings, O the diction, O the harmony, O the composition!

Death, then, is rest, and to rest the night is fitting. Therefore I think it fitting that in the night the burials of the dead be carried out, since to do any such thing by day must be avoided for many reasons. One man turns to one business about the city, another to another, and everything is full of men going to the courts, or to the marketplace and from the marketplace, or sitting at their crafts, or frequenting the temples that they may confirm the good hopes that come from the gods; and then certain persons, having laid a corpse upon a bier, force their way through the midst of those busied with these things. And the matter is in every way intolerable. For those who meet it are often filled with displeasure, some thinking the omen evil, while to those who are going to the temples it is not lawful to draw near before they have washed. For to the gods who are the authors of life, and of all things most alien to corruption, it is not lawful to draw near after such a sight. And I have not yet brought my heaviest charge against what is done. And what is this? The sacred enclosures and temples of the gods stand open; and often someone within is sacrificing and pouring libation and praying, while others pass close by the very temple, carrying a corpse, and the voice of lamentation and ill-omened cries is borne even to the altars.

From Litarbae I journeyed to Beroea, and Zeus gave all favourable signs, showing me a clear token from heaven. Staying there a day, I saw the citadel, and I sacrificed to Zeus, after the royal manner, a white bull, and I discoursed a little with the council on piety. But all praised my words, while very few were persuaded by them, and these only such as even before my words seemed to be soundly minded. They were cautious, as it were, to put off and lay aside their reverence for frankness; for it remains, O gods, among men to blush at noble things—at courage of soul and at piety—and to plume themselves, as it were, on the basest—on sacrilege, and on softness of mind and body.

I came from Pannonia this third year now, scarcely saved from the dangers and labours you know of. And having crossed the Calchedonian strait and halted at the city of Nicomedes, to you first, as to an ancestral god, I rendered the first-fruits of my own deliverance, sending to you, as a token of my arrival, in place of a sacred offering, my greeting. And the bearer of the letter was one of the imperial guards, Julian by name, son of Bacchylus, an Apamean by birth, to whom I entrusted the letter especially because he undertook both to come to you and to know you well. After this there came to me from you, as from Apollo, a sacred letter, making plain that you had gladly heard of our arrival; and this was to me a happy omen and the beginning of good hopes—Iamblichus the wise, and the letters of Iamblichus to us. Why need I tell how I rejoiced, or signify what I felt about the letter? For if you received what was written by us on this account—it was sent to you by a courier from those who had come from there—you fully knew, from what they made plain, how great a pleasure I had in them. Again, when the tutor of my children was returning home, I began another letter to you, at once confessing my gratitude for the former ones and asking the return in equal measure for the future. After this the fair Sopater came to us as an envoy; and I, when I knew it, at once leapt up and rushed out, and, embracing him, wept for joy, dreaming of nothing else but you and the letters from you to us. And when I received them, I kissed them and held them to my eyes, and clung to them fast, as though fearing that, in the reading of the letters, the image of your likeness might fly away from me unawares. And indeed I wrote back at once, not to you only but also to the holy Sopater, his son, as though making much of it that we had received the common comrade from Apamea as a kind of pledge for your absence. Since then, having now written to you a third time, I have myself received no other letter than the one in which you seem to reproach me.

As for the number one hundred, that it is more honourable than the others and circumscribes within itself the perfection of numbers, one might learn by considering thus. And I am not ignorant that it is the saying of men of old and wise, that the odd is set before the even, nor that they say the beginning of increase is the uncombined; for the like, abiding with the other, remains such as the other is, but when two have come to be, the third is the oddness. But I, even if the saying be too bold, would say nevertheless: the numbers are altogether dependent upon a beginning, and would carry continually their successive increase; yet I think it far juster to assign the cause of increase to the even rather than to the odd. For the number one could not be odd, having nothing in respect to which it might become odd; but the conjunction of the dyad gives birth to a twofold oddness, and from the two numbers the third reasonably comes to increase. And again, in the mixture of another dyad, it takes the excess of the tetrad; and in general the fellowship of the numbers with one another, showing the oddness from each, is enclosed within the number of the dyad. This being granted, I would say, I think, that, the first decad rolling round its revolution into itself, the whole passes over into the number of the hundred, so that, while the increase from the one would extend to ten, again the decad, ascending through itself, is completed into the number of the hundred. And thence again, from hundreds, the whole reaps the power of numbers, the one never resting, unless the dyad in the mixture ever begets the odd and recalls it again into itself, until once more, by another hundred, it shut up the gathered sum of the numbers, and, attaching to it perfection, creep again from it toward the other, by the appellations of hundreds ever carrying up the whole to the infinity of comprehension. And it seems to me that Homer too, neither simply nor idly, in his verses set about Zeus the aegis with its hundred tassels, but riddled this with some higher and unspeakable meaning, saying, as it were, that to the most perfect god he attached the most perfect number, and that with which alone, beyond the others, he might more justly be adorned; or because the whole universe, which he comprehended into the figure of the aegis by the roundness of the image, no other number circumscribes than the number of the hundred, fitting to the comprehension of the whole intelligible the hundred that runs in a circle. This same argument also seats the hundred-handed Briareus beside Zeus as his assessor, and allows him to contend against the power of the father, giving him, as it were, in the perfection of the number, the perfection of his strength. And further, Pindar the Theban, proclaiming in his epinicians the slaying of Typhoeus, and attributing the conquest of this greatest of giants to the greatest king of the gods, confirms the surpassing greatness of his eulogy from no other source than this, that he sufficed to bring down the hundred-headed giant with a single blow; as though no other giant were thought to have come to the hand of Zeus as an antagonist than him whom his mother alone of all armed with a hundred heads, nor any other of the gods more worthy of victory for the overthrow of so great a giant than Zeus alone. And to Simonides the lyric poet, for the praise of Apollo, it suffices to call the god "Hekatos" (god of the hundred), and, as it were in place of some other sacred token, to adorn him with the name, because, they say, he subdued the Python, the serpent, with a hundred arrows, and that he rejoices to be called Hekatos rather than Pythian, addressed, as it were, by the symbol of some perfect appellation. And the island that nursed Zeus, Crete, as though having received the nursing in return for her reception of Zeus, has been honoured with the number of a hundred cities. And Thebes too, the hundred-gated, Homer praises for no other reason than this, that in its hundred gates there was a wondrous beauty. And I pass over the hecatombs of the gods, and temples a hundred feet long, and altars with a hundred steps, and the men's halls that hold a hundred, and the fields of a hundred plethra, and all the other things, divine and human, that are comprised under the appellation of this number. This number, indeed, knows how to adorn both the military order and the order of peace, and it brightens the company of a hundred men under their captain, and honours, too, the bench of judges that comes to the same equal number. And though I have more than these to say, the law of the letter turns me back; but do you grant pardon to my discourse, because even these things have been said beyond what is sufficient. And if the attempt has any moderate beauty, in your judgement, it shall by all means be made open to the rest also, receiving the witness of your vote; but if it needs another hand for the filling-up of the aim, who could better than you, having refined the writing to beauty, polish it to the pleasure of the beholder?

Above all, then, we must practise love of mankind, for from this follow many other blessings, and in particular that choicest and greatest of all, the goodwill of the gods. For just as those who share their masters' interests in friendship and earnest pursuits and affection are loved more than their fellow-slaves, so we must believe that the Divine, being by nature loving toward mankind, loves those men who are loving toward their fellows. Now love of mankind is wide and of many kinds: it shows itself in punishing men with restraint, for the betterment of those punished, as teachers do with children; and in correcting their needs, as the gods correct ours. See how many good things they have given us out of the earth, foods of every sort, and more than they have given to all the animals together. And since we were born naked, they sheltered us with the hair of animals, and with what grows from the earth and from the trees. And it did not suffice them to do this simply or roughly, as Moses says we took coats of skins, but see how many are the gifts of Athena the Worker. What animal uses wine? What animal uses oil? None, except those to which we ourselves impart a share of them, we who give no share to our fellow-men. What creature of the sea uses corn, what creature of the land uses the things of the sea? I have not yet spoken of gold and bronze and iron, in all of which the gods have made us very rich; yet not that we may suffer the poor to wander about in reproach to the gods, especially when some of them happen to be reasonable in character, men to whom no inheritance has fallen from their fathers, and who, through their greatness of soul desiring money least of all, are poor. The multitude, seeing such men, reproach the gods. But the gods are not the cause of their poverty; rather the insatiable greed of us who possess wealth becomes the cause both of a false opinion about the gods among men, and besides of an unjust reproach against the gods. For why do we demand that the god should rain gold upon the poor, as he did upon the Rhodians? Even if this should happen, we should quickly set our servants under it and put out our vessels everywhere and drive everyone else away, so that we alone might seize the common gifts of the gods. And one might well marvel that, while we claim a thing which neither comes to pass by nature and would be wholly unprofitable, we do not do the things that are within our power. For who ever became poor by giving to his neighbours? Indeed I have often given to those in need, and have received it back from the gods many times over, although I am a poor man of business; and I have never repented of having given. As for the present, I will not speak of it; for it would be altogether unreasonable to compare the gifts of private men with the bounties of a king. But while I was still a private man, I am conscious that this often happened to me. My grandmother's inheritance came to me intact, though others held it by force, when out of the little I had I was spending and giving to those in need.
To his fellow-students, on Aristotle and Plato

If anyone has persuaded you that there is anything more pleasant or more profitable for men than to pursue philosophy at leisure and without distraction, he is deceived and deceives you. But if the old zeal still abides with you, and has not, like a bright flame, been quickly quenched, then I count you happy. The fourth year has now gone by, and this is now nearly the third month upon it, since we were parted from one another. I should be glad to consider how far in this time you have advanced. As for my own case, it is a wonder if I can still speak Greek; so far have we been barbarised by the regions where we live. Do not despise the lesser studies, neither neglect rhetoric nor association with the poets. But let your care for learning be greater, and let your whole labour be the knowledge of the doctrines of Aristotle and Plato. Let this be your work, this your foundation-stone, your base, your building, your roof; the rest are by-works, yet to be carried out by you with greater earnestness than others bestow on what are truly their works. I, by the divine Justice, loving you as brothers, give you this counsel; for you have been my fellow-students and my dear friends. If, then, you are persuaded, I shall love you the more; but if I see you disobedient, I shall be grieved. And what continued grief is wont in the end to come to, I forbear to say, for the sake of a better omen.

As for my dealings with him, the gods know that often, when he had wronged the provincials, I kept silence beyond what was fitting for me, hearing some things not at all, others not admitting, disbelieving others, and turning some of them upon his associates. But when he thought fit to make me a partner in such disgrace by sending me his foul memoranda, worthy of every shame, what was I to do? Was I to keep silence or to fight? The first was foolish and slavish and hateful to the gods; the second was just and brave and worthy of a free man, but not permitted by the affairs that held me fast. What, then, did I do? In the presence of many whom I knew would report it to him, I said: "This fellow will by all means and altogether revise his memoranda, since he conducts himself shamefully." When he heard this, so far was he from doing anything with self-control that he did such things as, by the god, no moderate tyrant would have done, and that with me so near at hand. Here what should a man do who is a follower of the doctrines of Plato and Aristotle? Was I to look on while wretched men were given over to thieves, or to defend them so far as I could, since already they were singing their swan-song because of that god-detested workshop of such men? For my part it seems shameful to me to condemn the tribunes when they leave their post—and yet those men ought to die at once and not even be thought worthy of burial—but to abandon my own post on behalf of these wretched men, when I must fight against such thieves, and that too with the god fighting at our side, the god who appointed us. And if anything should happen to me, with a good conscience it is no small consolation to depart. As for the good Sallust, may the gods grant him to me. And even if through this I should chance to be given a successor, it will perhaps grieve me not at all; for it is better to do well for a little while than ill for a long time. The doctrines of the Peripatetics are not, as some say, less noble than those of the Stoics; they differ only this much from one another, as I judge: the latter are always more heated and more headstrong, the former more worthy of prudence and more constant to their convictions.

Many things, indeed, come upon me besides these, but I must reserve some for your coming. Come, then, in the name of the gods, with all speed, using two carriages or more. And I have sent two of my most trusted servants, of whom one shall escort you as far as the camp, while the other shall announce that you have set out and are already arriving. Tell the young men yourself by which of them you wish each thing to be done.

These are the two things I promised to tell you; but a third, coming into my mind, I think I ought not to pass over in silence. The same man followed me to the Achilleum also, and showed me the tomb in good preservation; yet I had been told that this too had been dug up by him. But he approached it with deep reverence. I saw these things myself. And I have heard from those who are now at enmity with him that he used also to pray secretly and to worship Helios. Would you not accept me even as a private man for a witness? Of each man's disposition toward the gods who could be more trustworthy witnesses than the gods themselves? Should we have made Pegasius a priest, if we had been conscious of any impiety in him toward the gods? But if in those times, whether reaching after power, or, as he often told us, in order to save the temples of the gods, he wrapped himself in those rags and feigned impiety so far as the name—for he has plainly nowhere done any wrong to the temples, save for a very few stones taken from a covering, that he might be able to save the rest—if we take this into account and are not ashamed to do to him the very things which Aphobius did, and which all the Galilaeans pray to see him suffer—if you give any heed to me, you will honour not this man only, but the others too who have come over, that they may the more readily obey us when we call them to good things, and the others may be the less glad. But if we drive away those who come of their own accord, no one will readily obey us when we summon them.
Let this be published to my fellow-citizens, the Alexandrians.

I am ready to aid Pessinus, if its people render the Mother of the gods gracious to them; but if they neglect her, they shall be not only blameless but—not to put it too bitterly—shall perhaps even feel our displeasure. "For it is not lawful for me to receive into my care, nor to pity, men who are hateful to the immortal gods." Persuade them, then, if they hold to my care, all together to become suppliants of the Mother of the gods.

And yet to the Corinthians one might reasonably add this question: whether they think it well to follow the customs of ancient Hellas, or rather those which they seem lately to have received from the imperial city. For if they cherish the dignity of the ancient customs, it befits not the Argives to contribute to Corinth more than the Corinthians to Argos; but if it is the rights now belonging to their city, since they received the Roman colony, on which they insist in claiming to have the more, we shall moderately beg of them not to think themselves greater than their fathers, nor to set aside what those men, having decided well, preserved as customs for the cities of Hellas, and to make innovations to the harm and hurt of their neighbours, especially as they use a more recent decision, and have for a windfall to their greed the negligence of the man who was allotted to plead the cause on behalf of the city of the Argives. For if he had allowed the suit to be carried outside Hellas, the Corinthians were likely to have less strength, and justice, examined, would have appeared ill served by the many and noble advocates by whom the judge, with the added dignity of the city, would in all likelihood have been shamed into giving this verdict.

Set the columns of Daphne before the rest. Take those from the palaces everywhere and bring them away, and set in their places those from the houses lately seized; and if even from these they should be lacking, let us use cheaper ones, of baked brick and plaster, faced outside with marble for the time. For that holiness is better than costliness, and holds much pleasure in life and in use for the right-minded, you yourself know.

This I have resolved to proclaim in particular to the city of the Bostrenes, because the bishop Titus and the clergy, in the petitions they presented, accused the multitude that was with them, as though they themselves were exhorting the multitude not to riot, while the multitude was rushing into disorder. At any rate, the very words which he dared to write I have appended to this edict of mine. They are: "Although the Christians are a match in number for the Hellenes, they are held in check by our exhortation that no one anywhere behave disorderly." These are the bishop's words concerning you. See how he says that your good order proceeds not from your own will; for, as he said, you are held in check, unwillingly, by his exhortations. Of your own accord, then, drive him from the city as your accuser, but be at concord, you the multitudes, with one another, and let no man oppose or wrong another; neither let those who err harm those who worship the gods rightly and justly, according to what has been handed down to us from of old; nor let you who worship the gods plunder the houses or rob those who have erred more from ignorance than from intent. By reason we ought to persuade and teach men, not by blows and outrage and the torment of the body. Again and often I exhort those who press on toward the true religion to do no wrong to the multitudes of the Galilaeans, nor to attack nor insult them. Rather we ought to pity than to hate those who fare ill in the greatest things; for the greatest of all good things in truth is reverence for the gods, and, on the contrary, of all evils, impiety. And it befalls those who have turned aside from the gods to the dead and to relics to pay this penalty; for as with those held by some sickness we feel pain, so with those released and set free by the gods we rejoice.

The benefits, then, which have come to your city in particular from the Olympian gods—to speak briefly, for such they are—I pass over for the most part because of their length. But the things given in common, every day, not to a few men nor to one race nor to one city, but to all the world together, by the gods who are manifest—how is it that you do not know them? Are you alone insensible of the light that descends from Helios? Are you alone ignorant that summer and winter come from him? Are you alone ignorant that all things are quickened and grow from him? And the Moon, who is from him and through him the fashioner of all things—do you not perceive of how many good things she is the author to the city? And of these gods you dare to worship not one; but Jesus, whom neither you nor your fathers ever saw, you think must needs be God the Word. But him whom from all eternity the whole race of men beholds and sees and reveres, and reverencing prospers—the great Helios, I mean, the living image, ensouled and intelligent and beneficent, of the intelligible Father . . . if you will be persuaded by my exhortation, lead yourselves back, even a little, toward the truth. For you will not err from the right road if you obey one who himself walked that other road until his twentieth year, and now, by the grace of the gods, has walked this one for twelve years.

But do you think your frankness worth, as the saying is, four obols? Do you not know that Thersites too spoke freely among the Hellenes, and that the wise Odysseus struck him with his sceptre, while Agamemnon cared less for the drunken insolence of Thersites than a tortoise cares for flies, as the proverb runs? Yet it is no great thing to rebuke others and to keep oneself free from rebuke. If you have a share in this portion, show it to us. When you were young, did you give a fair account of yourself to your elders? But I, like Electra in Euripides, "pass over such fortunes in silence." But when you became a man and joined the camp, how did you act, in the name of Zeus? You say that, for the truth's sake, you gave offence and were dismissed. From what can you show this, as though it were not by many and most wicked men, by whom you yourself were driven out, that they too were banished? It is not the part of an earnest and self-controlled man, O most sagacious Dionysius, to depart in hatred from his rulers. You would have been better, if you had made men more moderate toward us by your company with them. But this is not in your power, by the gods, nor in the power of ten thousand others who emulate your manner; for rocks dashed against rocks, and stones against stones, do not help one another, but the stronger easily crushes the weaker.

Do you not know that, before all else, the works of the day and of the night are divided? Naturally, then, this is taken from the one and assigned to the other. For surely it is not right to forbid white among one's clothing during mourning, and yet to bury the dead by day and in the light. The other course were better, if no offence at all were thereby given to any of the gods; but this does not escape being an impiety toward all the gods. For to the Olympians men assign what they ought not, and from the gods of the underworld—or however else those who govern and are lords over souls rejoice to be named—they alienate, against right, what is theirs. I know that those who are scrupulous and exact in divine things hold it right to perform the rites to the gods below by night, or at any rate after the tenth hour of the day. But if this is the better season for the worship of those gods, neither shall we assign to the service of the dead a different one.

Thence Batnae received me, a place such as I never saw among you except Daphne, which now resembles Batnae; for of late, while the temple and the statue were still preserved, I should not be ashamed to set Daphne on a level with Ossa and Pelion and the peaks of Olympus and the Thessalian Tempe, or even to prefer her above all of them together. But concerning Daphne a discourse has been written by you, such as no other of those who are now mortals, even if he set himself earnestly to toil, could produce; and I think not many of the men of old, either. Why then do I now attempt to write of her, when so brilliant a monody has been composed upon her? Would that it had never been needed! Now Batnae—a barbarous name this—is a Hellenic place, first because through all the country round vapours of frankincense rose on every side, and everywhere we saw victims made ready. This, indeed, though it pleased me greatly, seemed nevertheless too warm, and foreign to true reverence toward the gods. For things sacred and holy toward the gods ought to be done apart from the throng, and in quiet, by men who come for this very purpose and not for any other. This, then, will perhaps presently obtain the care that fits it.

If, then, you accuse me for this reason, that under the form of a charge you may procure for us more occasions of writing, I receive the reproach very gladly, and in what I receive I appropriate to myself the whole of the favour; but if you truly accuse me of having fallen short in some duty toward you, who could be more wretched than I, through the injustice or sloth of letter-carriers, when I least of all men deserve to meet with this? And yet I, even if I do not write often, am justly worthy of pardon from you—not, I would say, because of the business I have in hand; may I never fare so ill as not to count your concerns above all business, as Pindar says—but because, toward so great a man, of whom even to make mention is awe, he who shrinks from writing is more temperate than he who is over-bold beyond what is fitting. For as those who dare to look continually at the dazzling rays of Helios, unless they be in some sort divine and, like the true-born of eagles, take courage against his beams, neither can behold what it is not lawful to see, and, the more they strive, the more they show that they cannot attain it, so too he who dares to write to you, the more he wishes to be bold, the more clearly he shows that he ought to fear. Yet for you, my noble friend, who are, one might say, the saviour of all the Hellenic world, it were fitting both to write to us ungrudgingly and to allay, so far as you can, the shrinking on our part. For as Helios—that the discourse may again take the image for you from the god—as Helios, then, when he shines whole with pure rays, withholds nothing from him who comes to his radiance, but does his own proper work, so too you ought, watering ungrudgingly the Hellenic world with your fair things as with light, not to shrink, if anyone, for shame or fear, is abashed at making the return to you. For neither does Asclepius heal men in hope of recompense, but everywhere fulfils his own loving-kindness. This you ought to do, being as it were a physician of cultured souls, and to preserve through all things the precept of virtue, like a good archer, who, even if he has no adversary, none the less ever exercises his hand toward the mark. Since the aim is not the same for both of us: ours is to obtain your good gifts, and yours to meet with what is given by us. But we, even if we write ten thousand times, play like the children of Homer, who, by the seashore, let whatever they have shaped of clay be washed away; whereas from you even a small letter is better than any fruitful stream, and I, for one, would rather possess one letter of Iamblichus than the gold of Lydia. If, then, you care anything for your lovers—and you do, unless I am mistaken—do not overlook us, who, like nestlings, ever stand in need of nurture from you; but write continually and do not shrink from feasting us with your fair things. And if we fall short, do you yourself appropriate the office of both, both of what you give and of what, on our behalf, you discharge in equal measure. It befits one who is a disciple, or, if you will, a foster-child, of Hermes the eloquent, not to keep that god's wand in sleeping, but rather to choose to imitate him in moving and rousing up.

We ought, then, to share our money with all men, but more freely with the good, and with the helpless and the poor so far as suffices for their need. And I would even say, though it sounds strange, that it would be a holy act to share clothing and food even with the wicked; for we give to the humanity in a man and not to his character. Therefore I think that even those shut up in prison are to be deemed worthy of such care. For such love of mankind will in no way hinder justice. Since many are confined awaiting trial, of whom some will be found guilty and others acquitted, it would be a hard thing, for the sake of the wicked, not to extend some pity also to the innocent, or, for the sake of the wicked, to be merciless and inhuman toward those who have done no wrong. And this, when I consider it, appears to me altogether unjust: we call Zeus the god of strangers, and yet we prove ourselves more inhospitable than the Scythians. How then does a man who wishes to sacrifice to Zeus the protector of strangers come to his temple? With what kind of conscience, having forgotten the verse: 'For from Zeus come all strangers and beggars; and a gift, though small, is welcome.'
To Maximus the philosopher

The divine Homer says there are two gates of dreams, and that the trust to be placed in them, concerning things to come, differs. But I think that you now, if ever before, have seen clearly concerning the future; for I myself beheld such a thing today. I dreamed that a tall tree, planted in some very large dining-hall, was leaning toward the ground, while beside its root there had grown another, small and newly sprung, very full of bloom. And I was greatly anxious about the little one, lest someone should tear it up along with the great one. And so, when I came near, I saw the great one stretched upon the ground, but the small one upright, raised above the earth. When I saw this, I said in distress: "Behold this great tree; there is danger lest not even its offshoot be saved." And one wholly unknown to me said: "Look carefully and take courage; for, since the root remains in the ground, the smaller tree will remain unharmed and will be more firmly established." Such, then, were the dreams; but God knows to what they tend.

But the rights on behalf of the city, and those of the advocates, if only you are willing to hear, and the pleading of the suit be entrusted to them, you shall learn from the beginning, and what occurs to one from what is said will be rightly judged. But that you ought to be persuaded, through us, by those who present this embassy, a little must be added concerning them. Diogenes and Lamprias are philosophers, if any among us are, but they have avoided the honoured and gainful parts of public life; ever eager, however, to aid their country to the best of their power, whenever the city falls into great need, then they make speeches and take part in affairs and go on embassies and spend gladly of their own substance, by their deeds making answer to the reproaches of philosophy, and proving false the opinion that those who pursue philosophy are useless to the cities. For their country uses them for these things, and they try to defend the right through us, and we again through you. For this alone is left to the wronged for their preservation, to obtain a judge who is both willing to judge and able to judge well; for whichever of these be lacking, the right, deceived or betrayed by him, must perish utterly. But since now we have judges according to our prayer, and yet they cannot plead unless leave was first granted, they ask that this first be conceded to them, and that the negligence of him who then pleaded for the city, and undertook the suit, may not become for her, for all time to come, the cause of so great a loss.

Concerning the affair with Lauricius I think I need write nothing to you, save only this counsel: put away all anger, commit everything to justice, lending your ears to his words with all good faith toward the right. And I do not say this as though the things written to you were not offensive and full of all insolence and contempt; but you must bear it; for it is the part of a good and great-souled man to be evil spoken of, but not to speak evil. For just as missiles hurled against solid and noble walls do not cling to them, nor strike, nor lodge, but recoil the more sharply upon those who throw them, so all reviling and slander and unjust insolence poured out upon a good man touches him not at all, but turns back upon him who pours it. This I counsel you; the rest shall be for the trial to decide. As for my letters, which he says you received from me and published, it seems to me laughable to bring them into court; for I, by the gods, never wrote to you, nor to any other man, anything which I do not wish to be set publicly before all. For what wantonness, what insolence, what abuse, what reviling, what foulness of speech, was ever written in my letters? Indeed, even if I felt harshly toward anyone, and the subject gave me leave to speak, as it were, "from the wagon," as Archilochus falsely did against Lycambes, I uttered it more gravely and more soberly than one who treats of a sacred theme. And if my letters showed the goodwill that exists between us, did I wish this to be hidden or concealed? Why? I have all the gods and goddesses to witness that even of all I wrote to my wife I should not have been vexed, had anyone published it; so full of self-control was it all. And if the letters I sent to my own uncle have been read by some one other man, by a second person, he who so bitterly tracked them down would more justly incur blame than I who wrote them, or you, or any other who read them. But, however, grant this and let it not trouble you; only consider this: Lauricius is a wicked man; deal with him nobly. But if he is reasonable and moderate, and offended against you, give him pardon; for the good, in public matters, even if privately they behave toward us not as they should, we ought to love. The wicked, in common affairs, even if they have done us a kindness, must be kept under hand—I do not say hated nor turned away from—but some guard must be set, that they may not work mischief unawares; and if they are hard to watch, then to make no use of them at all. As for the man of whom you yourself also wrote, that, being notorious for wickedness, he plays the physician, he was summoned by us as an earnest man; but before he came into our sight he was detected for what he was, or rather informed against; and by whom I will tell you when I meet you. He was held in scorn; and for this too I am grateful to you.
Given on the Kalends of August, at Antioch.

If, then, it is your pleasure to obey, you will rejoice the more; but if you choose to abide in the superstition and instruction of cunning men, at least be at concord among yourselves, and do not long for Athanasius. There are surely many of his disciples able sufficiently to soothe your ears that itch and crave impious words. Would that, together with Athanasius, the wickedness of his impious school had been shut up. But as it is, you have a multitude not ignoble, and there is no trouble at all. For whomever of the multitude you choose, so far at least as concerns the exposition of the Scriptures, he will be in no way worse than the one you long for. But if it is for the rest of Athanasius' cleverness that you love him—for I learn that the man is a cunning fellow—and for this reason made these petitions, know that for this very thing he has been banished from the city; for a meddlesome man is by nature unfit to be the head of a people. And if he be not even a man, but a paltry manikin, like this great fellow who thinks his head is in danger, this gives the beginning of disorder. Therefore, that no such thing may happen to you, we long ago bade him depart from the city, and now from all Egypt as well.

Do I say this in Laconian and brief fashion? Yet I think that, because of you, I have shown myself more talkative even than the Attic cicadas. As for the wanton things you have said against me, I will lay upon you a fitting penalty, the gods willing, and the lady Adrasteia. What, then, is the penalty, and what most can pain your tongue and your mind? I will try, by erring as little as possible in word and deed, to give your slanderous tongue no great occasion for chatter. And yet it has not escaped me that even Aphrodite's sandal, they say, was mocked by Momus. But you see that Momus too burst with much effort, and could scarce lay hold even of the sandal. May it be yours, too, growing old while you rub at such things, to outlive Tithonus, and to be richer than Cinyras, and more luxurious than Sardanapalus, that the proverb may be fulfilled in you: "Old men are twice children."

For those who willingly obey, this suffices. For having learned in what they erred, let them change to the better. But if anyone is such as to need threat and penalty, let him know that he shall undergo the heaviest punishment, if before the tenth hour of the day he dares to tend the body of any of the departed and carry it through the city. Rather let these things be done after the sun has set, and again before he rises; and let the day, pure, be set apart for pure works and for the Olympian gods.

Batnae I found a wooded plain holding groves of young cypresses; and among them there was no aged or rotten tree, but all alike flourishing in their foliage; and the palace was by no means costly, for it was of clay only and wood, with nothing of variety; but the garden, inferior to that of Alcinous, yet like that of Laertes, and in it a very small grove, full of cypresses, and along the wall many such trees planted in rows, one after another. Then in the midst were garden-beds, and in these vegetables, and trees bearing fruit of every kind. What, then, did I do there? I sacrificed in the evening, and again at deep dawn, as I am wont to do fairly every day. And since the sacrifices were favourable, we held on toward the Holy City, and the citizens came to meet me, and a stranger received me, seen but lately, but loved by me long since. The reason you yourself, I well know, share in the knowledge of, but it is pleasant to me to tell it even so; for to hear and to speak of such things is to me as nectar. Sopater, the kinsman of the most divine Iamblichus, was his connexion by marriage; for to me it seems no less a wrong than any of the basest not to love all the affairs of those men. There is a greater reason still. For, having often received my cousin and my brother by the same father, and being often urged by them, as was natural, to forsake reverence toward the gods—which is a hard thing—he was not caught by the disease.

And how does the man who worships Zeus the god of comradeship, when he sees his neighbours in want of money, and gives them not so much as a drachma, think that he is rightly worshipping Zeus? When I look upon these things I am utterly at a loss; for I see that the titles of the gods have been with us from the beginning of the world, like painted images, but that in practice nothing of the kind is observed by us. Among us the gods are called kindred, and Zeus the god of kindred, yet we treat our own relations as strangers. For every man is the kinsman of every man, whether he will or no, whether, as some say, we are all sprung from one man and one woman, or whether it came about in some other way, the gods having created us all at once, together with the world at its first beginning, not one man and one woman but many men and many women together. For those who had power to create one man and one woman were able also to create many men and many women at once; for in the same way that they made the one man and the one woman, in that same way they made the many men and the many women. And one should look also to the diversity of customs and laws; and, what is greater and more honourable and more authoritative, to the report of the gods, which has been handed down to us by the ancient theurgists: that when Zeus was ordering all things, there fell drops of sacred blood, and from these, it would seem, the race of men sprang up. And so we are all kinsmen, whether being many men and women we are sprung from one man and one woman, or whether, as the gods say and as we must believe since the facts bear witness, we are all sprung from the gods. That the facts bear witness that many men came into being at once will be set forth elsewhere with precision; here it suffices to say so much, that if we were sprung from one man and one woman it is not likely that the laws would differ so widely, nor again that one man could have filled the whole earth, not even if the women bore them many children at once, like sows. But since the gods planted us everywhere at once, in the same way that the one man came forth, so also did the many men come forth, allotted to the gods who are the founders of races, who brought them forth, receiving their souls from the Demiurge from all eternity.
To Eustathius

Just when I had recovered from a very grievous and harsh illness, by the providence of him who watches over all things, your letter came into my hands, on the very day I first bathed. In the evening, having read it, you could not easily say how I was strengthened, perceiving your pure and unalloyed goodwill; of which may I become worthy, that I may not disgrace your friendship. Your letters I read at once, though I was scarcely able to do so; but those of Antoninus to Alexander I reserved for the morrow. From there, on the seventh day, I write this to you, my recovery proceeding by degrees through the forethought of God. Be kept safe for me, most longed-for and most beloved brother, by the god who watches over all things; may I see you, my good friend. And in my own hand: By your safety and mine, by the god who watches over all things, I have written as I think. Best of men, when shall I see you and embrace you? For now I love even your name, like those who are sick with love.

And one ought not to think it strange that the suit should be made open again; for private men it is profitable to overlook a little the better and more advantageous, buying security for the time to come; for, their life being short, it is pleasant to enjoy even a little quiet, while it is fearful to be ruined in the courts in litigation, and to hand down to one's children a suit unfinished; so that it is perhaps better to gain the half in any way than, contending for the whole, to die. But the cities, being immortal, if someone judging justly does not free them from their strife with one another, must of necessity keep their ill-will immortal, and their hatred, strong and strengthened by time. It has been said, the orators say, this is my plea; but you yourself will judge what is right.

As for the lands you asked for, since I have already given those away—the gods of kindred and of friendship are my witnesses—I will give you others far more profitable, and you yourself shall perceive it.
Let this be published to our fellow-citizens, the Alexandrians.

But that wondrous Alexander—from what did he appear to you so great? Is it because, having become his imitator, you emulated all that the lad Hermolaus reproached him with? Or is no one so foolish as to suspect this of you? On the contrary, that very thing which Hermolaus bewailed as having suffered, and for which, they say, he plotted to kill Alexander—is there anyone who is not persuaded of this about you? By the gods, I have heard many who say they love you greatly making many apologies for this fault, while one even disbelieved it. But this is the one swallow; it does not make the spring. Or perhaps Alexander seemed to you great for this, that he bitterly slew Callisthenes, that Cleitus fell a victim to his drunken violence, that Philotas, and Parmenio, and Parmenio's son perished. For of the affairs of Hector, who was drowned in Egypt in the eddies of the Nile or of the Euphrates—for both are told—and of his other amusements, I say nothing, lest I seem to slander a man who, though by no means a model of right conduct, was yet a most excellent general in war. Of these things you, in purpose and in courage, have less share than fishes have of hair. Hear, then, the counsel—do not too angrily—"Not to you, my child, are warlike deeds given." What follows I do not write out for you, for I am ashamed, by the gods. Yet I bid you supply it yourself; for it is reasonable that words should follow deeds, and that he who has in no way escaped the deeds should not shun the words.

These things I had to write to you from the Holy City concerning my own affairs. As for the military and civil administration, you ought, I think, to oversee and care for them yourself, being present; for the matter is greater than a letter, be assured, and so great that it is not easy to compass the precise account even in thrice the length of this. These too I will tell you summarily, in few words. I sent envoys to the Saracens, reminding them to come if they would. So much for one thing. As for another, I sent out men as wakeful as possible to keep watch, lest anyone slip away from here to the enemy to be an informer of our movements. From there I judged a military case, as I am persuaded, most gently and most justly. I provided spare horses and mules, gathering the army together to one place. River boats are being filled with corn, or rather with dried bread and vinegar. And how each of these was done, and what discussions arose over each, you can imagine of what length the writing would be. And as for all the letters and books to which I have set my hand—for these too follow me about everywhere like a shadow—why need I trouble myself now to count them up?

And this too is worth considering, how many discourses have been spent by men of old upon the doctrine that man is by nature a social animal. Shall we, then, who have said and ordained these things, behave unsociably toward those near to us? Therefore let each of us, setting out from such habits and pursuits, from reverence toward the gods, from kindness toward men, from purity of body, fulfil the works of piety; let him strive always to think reverently of the gods, and look with honour and holiness upon their temples and images, worshipping them as though he saw the gods present. For our fathers established images and altars and the keeping of an unquenchable fire, and in a word all such things, as symbols of the presence of the gods; not that we should regard these things as gods, but that through them we should worship the gods. For since, being in the body, it was necessary for us to render our service to the gods also in a bodily fashion, whereas the gods themselves are without body, the gods showed us, as a first race after the first gods, the images that are carried round in a circle throughout all the heaven. But since not even to these can worship be rendered bodily, for they are by nature in need of nothing, another race of images was devised on earth, in performing whose worship we shall render the gods gracious toward us. For just as those who tend the images of kings, though the kings need nothing, nevertheless draw goodwill upon themselves, so too those who tend the images of the gods, though the gods need nothing, nevertheless persuade them to defend and care for them. For zeal in what is possible is a true proof of holiness, and he who fulfils this evidently renders the gods the greater honour, while he who neglects what is possible, and then pretends to reach after the impossible, plainly is not pursuing the one but disregarding the other. For even if the god needs nothing, it does not follow that on that account we should offer him nothing; for neither does he need the praise that comes through words. What then? Is it reasonable to deprive him even of this? By no means. Neither, then, should we deprive him of the honour rendered to him through deeds, which not three years nor three thousand years established, but all the ages that have gone before, among all the nations of the earth.
To Eustathius

Syloson, they say, went up to Darius and reminded him of the cloak, and asked of him, in return for it, Samos. Thereupon Darius prided himself, thinking he had given great things in return for small, while Syloson received a gift that brought him grief. Consider now my case beside his. In one thing, I think, my deed is the better: I did not wait to be reminded by another; but having kept the memory of your friendship unimpaired through so long a time, as soon as God gave me the power, I summoned you back not among the second but among the first. So much, then, for the past. But concerning the future, will you grant me—for I am something of a prophet—to foretell? I think it far better than the other, and may Adrasteia be gracious. For you have no need of a king to help you overturn a city, while I have need of many to help me set right what has fallen ill. These things the Gallic and barbarous Muse plays with you; but may you come rejoicing under the escort of the gods. And in his own hand: A spoil of kids, and of the hunting of the lambs in the winter quarters. Come to your friend, who even then, though not yet able to know what manner of man you are, nevertheless cherished you.

But you who pretend to honour the memory of Magnentius and Constans—why do you war against the living and revile those who are in any way the best? Is it because the dead are better able to defend themselves against those who grieve them than the living? But this you cannot say; for you are, as you write, most full of confidence. But if not this, then perhaps something else; for you do not wish, it may be, to mock those who would feel it. Yet of the living, is anyone so foolish or small-minded as to think it worth his while to be reckoned of any account by you, and not rather to wish, most of all, to be wholly unknown to you, or, if that be impossible, to be reviled by you, as I am now, rather than honoured? May I never be so ill-minded; may I never lay claim to praise from you rather than blame.

Looking, then, upon the images of the gods, let us not suppose them to be stones or wood, nor yet that they are the gods themselves. For neither do we call the images of the kings wood and stone and bronze, nor yet the kings themselves, but images of kings. Whoever, then, is a lover of his king looks with pleasure on the image of his king, and whoever is a lover of his child looks with pleasure on the image of his child, and whoever is a lover of his father, on the image of his father. So too whoever is a lover of the gods looks with pleasure on the images and likenesses of the gods, revering at the same time and trembling before the gods who from the unseen look upon him. If, then, anyone thinks that, because they have once been called images of the gods, they must not be capable of being destroyed, he seems to me wholly senseless. For surely they ought not to have come into being by the hands of men at all. But what has come into being by the hand of a wise and good man can be destroyed by a wicked and ignorant man. The living images, however, which the gods fashioned out of their unseen substance, namely the gods who are borne in a circle round the heaven, abide for ever and are everlasting. Let no one, then, disbelieve in the gods because he sees and hears that certain men have committed outrage against the images and the temples. Have not many slain good men, such as Socrates and Dion and the great Empedotimus? Yet I am well assured that the gods cared more for these than for the temples. But you see that, knowing the body of these men too to be perishable, the gods allowed it to yield to nature and give way, but exacted the penalty afterward from those who slew them. And this has plainly come to pass in our own day in the case of all who have plundered temples.
To Eustathius

I had already recovered from my illness when you sent the geography; nevertheless I received the little tablet sent by you with no less pleasure on that account. For it has the diagrams better than the former ones, and you have set it to music by adding the iambics, not singing the battle of Bupalus, after the manner of the Cyrenaean poet, but such as the fair Sappho wishes to fit to her songs. The gift is such as it perhaps befitted you to give and was most pleasant for me to receive. As for the administration of affairs, we rejoice with you that you are eager to carry everything through both vigorously and gently. For to blend gentleness and self-control with courage and strength, and to use the one toward the most reasonable men and the other relentlessly, for their correction, toward the wicked, is the work of no mean nature nor of slight virtue, as I am persuaded. We pray that you, holding to both these aims, may harmonise them into the one end, the good; for this, not without reason, the wisest of the ancients believed to be the goal set before all the virtues. May you continue in health and prosperity for the longest time, most longed-for and most beloved brother.

But this very thing, that I write to you, is perhaps the act of one who is stung? No, by the saviour gods, but of one who checks your excessive arrogance and audacity, and the licence of your tongue, and the savagery of your soul, and the madness of your wits, and your derangement in all things. For it was in my power, had I been stung, to chastise you by deeds, not words, in quite lawful fashion. For, being a citizen and a member of the senate, you refused an emperor's command; and this surely was not permitted to one who had no great necessity to plead. It would not, then, have sufficed me to fine you on this account with every kind of penalty, but I thought I ought first to write to you, supposing the case curable by a short letter. But when I found you persisting in the same course, or rather detected the madness that until now lay hidden . . . lest you be thought a man, when you are no man, and full of frankness, when you are full of stupidity, and to have shared in education, when you have not touched even a syllable of letters, so far as it is reasonable to conjecture from your letters. For "vanished" no one of the ancients used of what is in plain sight, as you now do; since the other faults of your letter no one could go through in a long book, nor that pandering and loathsome character by which you play the pander to yourself. For you say that we ought to choose, not those who come ready to hand, nor those who lie in wait for office, but those who use steadfast judgement, and on this account choose what is needful, and not those who obey readily. A fair hope you hold out to us, who need it not, that you will yield, if again we should call you to a share in affairs! But so far is this from me, that, while others were admitted, I never even addressed a word to you. And yet I did this toward many of my acquaintance, and of men unknown to me, who dwell in god-beloved Rome. So earnestly did I lay claim to your friendship, so worthy of esteem did I think you. It is likely, then, that what is to come toward you will be of the same kind. For even now I have written this letter, not for you alone to read, since I knew it would be needful for many; and I will give it to all, who will receive it, as I am persuaded, not unwillingly; for, seeing you graver and more puffed up than the life you formerly led, they are vexed.

Let no one, then, deceive us with words nor disturb us concerning providence. For those who reproach us on this account, the prophets of the Jews, what will they say of their own temple, which was overthrown three times and is not being raised even now? This I say not as a reproach to them, since I myself, after so long a time, intended to restore it, in honour of the god whose name is invoked over it. But in this instance I have used it because I wish to show that nothing human can be imperishable, and that the prophets who wrote such things talked nonsense, conversing with foolish old women. Yet nothing, I think, prevents the god from being great, though he did not chance upon worthy prophets or interpreters. The reason is that they did not give their souls leave to be purified by the regular course of studies, nor to open their eyes that were tight shut, nor to clear away the mist that lay upon them; but, like men who see a great light through a fog, not clearly nor purely, and who suppose that very thing to be not pure light but fire, and being blind to all that lies about it, they cry aloud: 'Tremble, be afraid, fire, flame, death, dagger, broadsword,' describing under many names the single destructive power of fire. But concerning these men it is better to show separately, in detail, how much worse than our own poets these teachers of doctrines about God have proved to be.
To Maximus the philosopher

All things rush upon me at once and shut up my voice, not suffering one thought to come forth before another, whether these be passions of the soul or whatever else one may please to call such things. But let us assign to them the order which time itself has assigned, having given thanks to the gods, who are the authors of all good, who have suffered me thus far to write, and perhaps will suffer us to see one another also.
