As soon as I became emperor—against my will, as the gods know—I made this plain there, on the spot, in such manner as I could; for, having taken the field against the barbarians, that campaign of mine lasting three months, on my return to the Gallic shores I kept watch and inquired of those who came from your parts whether any philosopher, any scholar wearing the cloak or the mantle, had landed. And when I was near Besontio—it is now a small town that has been restored, but of old it was great and adorned with costly temples, and with a strong wall, and besides with the natural strength of the place; for the river Doubs runs round it, and it stands up like a rocky headland in the sea, all but inaccessible, I might almost say, even to the birds, except where the river, flowing round it, affords as it were some beaches lying before it—near this city there met me a certain Cynic, wearing the threadbare cloak and carrying a staff. Seeing him from afar, I supposed him to be no other than you; and when I came nearer I thought he had certainly come from you. The man was indeed a friend, but he fell short of my expectation. This, then, was one such dream of mine. After this, I thought you would by all means be inquiring into my affairs, and that you could nowhere be found outside Greece. Let Zeus be my witness, and great Helios, and the might of Athena, and all the gods and goddesses, how, as I came down upon Illyricum from among the Celts, I trembled for you. And I inquired of the gods—not daring to do so myself, for I could not endure to see or hear any such thing as one might suppose was happening to you then, but committing it to others; and the gods clearly showed that there would be certain disturbances about you, but nothing dreadful, nor any accomplishment of those godless designs.

You have from us a complete answer, so that you need long for nothing more. Neither, then, do we ask anything further from you; but, having read it, use the letter for whatever you wish; for the matter of our friendship is at an end for you. Farewell, living in luxury and reviling me, much as ever.

It is fitting to worship not only the images of the gods, but also the temples and sacred precincts and altars. And it is reasonable to honour the priests too, as ministers and servants of the gods, who minister to us in our concerns toward the gods, and who lend their aid in the gift of good things that comes to us from the gods; for they sacrifice and pray on behalf of all. It is just, therefore, to render to them all honour no less than, if not more than, to the civil magistrates. And if anyone thinks that we ought to assign this equally to them and to the civil magistrates, since these too in a way serve the gods as priests, being guardians of the laws, still in respect of goodwill we ought to render far more to the priests. For the Achaeans bade their king reverence the priest even when he was an enemy; but we do not even reverence our friends who pray and sacrifice on our behalf.
To Maximus the philosopher

At the beginning of the third hour of the night, having not even a secretary, since all are busy, I have scarcely been able to write this to you. We live, by the gods, set free from suffering or doing irreparable things. Let Helios be my witness, whom above all I besought to aid me, and Zeus the king, that never did I pray to slay Constantius, but rather prayed against it. Why then did I come? Because the gods plainly bade me, promising safety if I obeyed, but, if I stayed, what may no god bring to pass; and besides, because, having been declared an enemy, I thought only to frighten him and to bring matters to a more reasonable understanding; but if it should be decided by battle, I committed everything to fortune and to the gods, and awaited whatever might seem good to their loving-kindness.

But since the discourse has come at last to the theme I have long desired, it seems to me worthwhile to set forth in order what kind of man the priest himself must be, that he may justly be honoured and may cause the gods to be honoured. For we ought not to regard or scrutinise his private conduct; but so long as a man is named a priest, we must honour and serve him; only, if he prove to be wicked, he must be deprived of the priesthood as one shown to be unworthy, and so disregarded. But while he sacrifices and conducts the rites and stands before the gods, we must look upon him with reverence and awe, as the most precious possession of the gods. For it would be absurd that, while we love the very stones of which the altars are made because they have been consecrated to the gods, since they have a shape and form fitted to the service for which they are made, we should think it right not to honour a man who has been consecrated to the gods. Perhaps someone will object: but what if he wrongs and offends in many things against piety toward the gods? I say that such a man must be exposed, lest, being wicked, he trouble the gods; but until someone exposes him, he must not be dishonoured. For it is not reasonable, taking hold of this pretext, to deprive of their honour not these men only but the worthy as well. Let every priest, then, like every magistrate, be held in reverence, since there is also a saying of this kind from the god of Didyma: 'All those who against the priests, in the wantonness of their minds, work folly against the immortals, and against their honours plot opposition with thoughts that fear not the gods, shall not pass through to the end the whole path of life, all those who have done outrage to the blessed gods, whose god-revered ministering honour those men have taken away.' And again in another place the god says: 'All my servants from baneful evil...' and he declares that for these things he will lay a penalty upon them.
To Maximus the philosopher

We live, saved by the gods; and do you sacrifice thank-offerings to them on my behalf. And you shall sacrifice not on behalf of one man only, but on behalf of the whole community of the Hellenes. And if you have leisure to cross over even as far as the city of Constantine, I should set no small value on your company.

Many such things having been said by the god, from which we may learn how we ought to honour and serve the priests, I shall speak of them more fully elsewhere. For the present it suffices, in order to prove that I am not improvising anything, to set forth the god's prophecy and command, holding the words of the god himself sufficient. If, then, anyone has supposed me a trustworthy teacher of such matters, let him, out of reverence for the god, obey him, and honour the priests of the gods above all. What kind of man the priest must be I shall now try to say, not for your sake; for, did I not know this already, with both my guide and the greatest gods bearing witness that you will administer this service well, so far at least as depends on your own choice, I should not have dared to entrust to you so great a matter. But it is that you may have wherewith to teach others, not only in the cities but also in the country districts, with the better reason and the greater authority, since you do not conceive and practise these things of yourself alone, but have me too as one who casts his vote with you, who am held, through the gods, to be supreme high priest, in no way worthy of so great an office, yet wishing to be so and ever praying to the gods that I may be. For be well assured, the gods hold out to us great hopes after death; and we must by all means believe them. For they are wont not to lie, and that not only concerning the things after death, but also concerning the things in this life. And those who, through abundance of power, are able to overcome the disorder of this life and to set right its confusion and disarray, shall they not still more, in that other state, where the warring elements are parted, when the immortal soul is separated and the dead body has become earth, be able to provide all that they have promised to men? Knowing, then, that the gods have given great rewards to the priests, let us make them in all things sureties of the worthiness of the gods; and this they must show to the multitudes by bringing forth their own life as a proof.
To Zeno

The chronicler of Thurii said that the ears of men are less to be trusted than their eyes. But concerning you I hold the contrary opinion; for my ears are more to be trusted by me than my eyes. For if I had seen you ten times over, I should not so have trusted my eyes as now I trust my own ears, having been taught by a man wholly incapable of falsehood that in everything, being a man, you surpass yourself "in achievement," as Homer says, "with hands and feet." Therefore, entrusting to you the use of arms, we have sent you a full suit of armour, such as befits the foot-soldiers; and we have enrolled you in the company of our own household troops.

We must begin with piety toward the gods. For we ought so to minister to the gods as though they stood beside us and saw us though we see them not, and as though, with an eye stronger than any sunbeam, they reached even to our hidden thoughts. And that this saying is not mine but the god's, having been declared in many oracles, it suffices me to bring forward one, and by means of it to establish two things at once, both how the gods see all things, and how they rejoice over the pious: 'Everywhere Phoebus' far-seeing ray is spread; and through the solid rocks his swift eye passes, and through the dark-blue sea it goes, nor does the starry multitude escape him, wheeling back as it returns to the unwearied heaven by the ordinance of wise necessity, nor all those tribes of the dead below that gloomy Tartarus received beneath the darkness of Hades; but in pious mortals I rejoice as much as in Olympus.'
To Eustathius

It is said that Alexander of Macedon used to sleep with the poems of Homer, that both by night and by day he might commune with his warlike maxims; but we sleep with your letters as with some healing remedies, and we do not cease reading them continually, always as though they were fresh and had but now first come into our hands. If, then, you are willing to procure for us, as an image of your presence, this converse through letters, write and do not leave off doing this continually; or rather, come, the gods willing, considering that, so long as you are absent, we cannot even say that we live, save in so far as we may read what is written by you.

And in proportion as every soul, and far more the soul of man, is more akin and more nearly related to the gods than stone and rock, so much the more readily and effectively, in all likelihood, does the eye of the gods pass through it. Consider, too, the love of the god for mankind, when he says that he rejoices in the mind of pious men as much as in Olympus, the purest of all things. How then shall he not raise up our souls also from the gloom and from Tartarus, if we draw near to him with piety? For he knows even those shut up in Tartarus, since not even they fall outside the power of the gods; and he promises Olympus to the pious instead of Tartarus. Therefore we must cling above all to the works of piety, drawing near to the gods with reverence, neither saying nor hearing anything shameful. And the priests must be pure not only from unclean deeds and licentious acts, but also from such words and from listening to such things. We must therefore banish all offensive jesting, all licentious talk. And that you may understand what I mean: let no man who has been consecrated read Archilochus or Hipponax or any other writer of such things. Let him turn aside also from the Old Comedy whatever is of this kind; for it is better so. And in every way philosophy alone would befit us, and of the philosophers those who set up the gods as guides of their own training, such as Pythagoras and Plato and Aristotle and the school of Chrysippus and Zeno. For we must attend neither to all of them nor to the doctrines of all, but only to those, and to those of their teachings, which are productive of piety and which teach concerning the gods, first that they exist, then that they care for the things here, and that they do no evil at all, neither to men nor to one another, out of envy and jealousy and hostility, of which sort the things our own poets wrote, and were despised for them, while the prophets of the Jews, who busily build up such teaching, are admired by these wretched men who have attached themselves to the Galilaeans.
To Eustathius

Grant me to say, after the manner of the melodious orators: "Oh, beyond hope am I preserved! Oh, beyond hope have I heard that you have escaped the three-headed hydra!" By Zeus, I do not mean my brother Constantius; he indeed was such as he was; but I mean the wild beasts about him, who cast their eyes greedily upon all men, and who made even him harsher, though of himself he was not altogether without gentleness, even if to many he seemed such. Of him, then, since he is now dead, let the earth lie light, as the saying is. But for these others I should not wish that anything should befall them unjustly—let Zeus be my witness. But since many accusers have risen up against them, a court has been appointed by lot. Do you, my friend, be present, and hasten beyond your strength; for I have long prayed by the gods to see you, and now, having most gladly heard that you are safe, I bid you come.

It would be fitting for us to read histories, all those that have been composed concerning deeds actually done; but as for those fictions which have been handed down by men of old in the form of history, we must avoid them, love-stories and all such things absolutely. For just as not every road is suited to the consecrated, but these too must be appointed, so neither is every kind of reading fitting for a consecrated man. For there comes to be in the soul a certain disposition from words, and little by little it stirs the desires, then suddenly kindles a terrible flame, against which, I think, we must be armed from afar.
To Prohaeresius the sophist

Why should I not greet the noble Prohaeresius, a man who pours forth speeches upon the young as rivers pour their streams upon the plains, and who rivals Pericles in eloquence, save in the matter of throwing Hellas into confusion and turmoil? You must not wonder that to you I have imitated Laconian brevity. For it befits you wise men to make speeches very long and great, but for us even brief words to you are enough. Know, then, that many affairs flow in upon me from every side. As for the causes of my return, if you write a history I will report them to you most precisely, furnishing the letters as written proofs; but if you have resolved to persevere to the end, even to old age, in your declamations and exercises, perhaps you will not blame my silence at all.

Let no Epicurean argument come in, nor any of Pyrrho; the gods, indeed, have already done well to destroy these, so that most of their books have perished. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent us mentioning these too, by way of example, of what kind of arguments the priests above all ought to keep away from; and if from arguments, far more from notions. For I do not think that an error of the tongue and an error of the mind are the same thing; rather we must tend above all the mind, since it is through the mind that the tongue too errs. We must learn by heart the hymns to the gods; and these are many and beautiful, composed by men ancient and recent. Yet we must try to know especially those that are sung in the temples. For most of these were given by the gods themselves in answer to entreaty, and some few were composed even by men, set together to honour the gods by a divine inspiration and a soul untrodden by evils.
To Aetius the philosopher

To all in general who were in any way banished by the late Constantius on account of the madness of the Galilaeans I have remitted their exile; but to you I not only remit it, but, remembering our old acquaintance and intimacy, I invite you to come to me. You shall use a public conveyance as far as my camp, and one spare horse.

These things at least are worth practising, and we must pray often to the gods, in private and in public, most of all three times a day, but if not, at any rate at dawn and at evening. For it is not reasonable that the consecrated should pass a day or a night without sacrifice; and dawn is the beginning of the day, evening of the night. It is reasonable to consecrate the first-fruits of both these portions to the gods, whenever we chance to be outside our priestly service; for as to the things in the temples, whatever the ancestral law prescribes, it is fitting to observe, and neither more nor less of them should be done; for the things of the gods are everlasting, so that we too must imitate their nature, that on this account we may the more propitiate them.
To Eustathius the philosopher

On receiving your letter I was glad, as was natural; for how should I not be, learning that a man who is my comrade and the dearest of friends is well? And how, when I had broken the seal upon it and read it over many times, I cannot put into words what manner of man I became; for, being filled with calm and gladness of heart, I embraced the letter as though I beheld in it some image of your noble character. To write of it in detail would be long, and perhaps not free from idle chatter. But what I especially approved I will not hesitate to say. First, that the outrage which the governor of Hellas committed against you—if indeed such a man ought to be called a governor and not a tyrant—you bore not heavily, deeming that none of these things had been done against you. Then, that you wished and were eager to help that city in which you made your sojourn—this is a plain proof of a philosophic mind; so that the former seems to me to befit Socrates, the latter, I think, Musonius. For the one said that it is not lawful for a good man to be harmed by any of his inferiors and worthless men, while the other cared for the people of Gyara when Nero sentenced him to exile there. Having praised these things in your letter, I do not know in what way I shall receive the third point. For you write, bidding me indicate whatever you may seem to me to do or say out of tune. But that I now think I myself have more need of such admonitions than you do, though I have much to say, I will defer to another time. The request perhaps does not befit you either; for you have leisure to spare, and you are well endowed by nature, and you love philosophy if any man ever did. And these three things, coming together, sufficed to make Amphion the discoverer of the ancient music—time, the breath of God, and love of song. For not even the lack of instruments has the power to oppose these; rather these too the man who shares in these three would readily discover. For have we not received it by tradition that this very man discovered not only the harmonies, but the lyre itself besides, whether by some more than human invention or by some divine gift through a help past finding out? And most of the men of old seem to have given especial heed to these three things, and to have philosophised, not in pretence, needing nothing else. You must, then, be present, and through your letters too exhort us eagerly as to what should and should not be done; for we see that even among soldiers it is not those who are at peace who need allies, but those, I think, who are toiling in the war; and that among pilots it is not those who are not sailing who summon those who sail, but those who are at sea call upon those who are at leisure. So from the beginning it has seemed just that those at leisure should defend and stand by those engaged in affairs and instruct them what should be done, whenever, I think, they have the same purpose. Considering this, you should do for me the very thing which you ask should be done by me toward you; and, if it please you, let us make this compact, that I shall signify to you whatever seems to me about all your affairs, and you in turn to me about my words and deeds; for nothing, I think, could be fairer for us than such an exchange. May divine providence keep you in health for many years, most longed-for brother. May I see you speedily, as I pray.

Now if we were souls alone, and the body troubled us in nothing, it would be well to mark off one single mode of life for the priests. But since it befits not priests in general, but the priest only at the time of his service, to practise certain things, what then should be conceded to the man who has obtained the priesthood, when he is outside the service in the temples? I think the priest ought, having kept himself pure from all things for a night and a day, and then for another night after that having purified himself with the purifications prescribed by the ordinances, so to enter within the temple and remain there for as many days as the law commands. Among us in Rome they are thirty, but elsewhere it is otherwise. It is reasonable, then, I think, to remain all these days in the temples, given to philosophy, and to go neither to a private house nor to the marketplace, nor even to see a magistrate except in the temples, but to attend to the service of the divine, overseeing and ordering everything; and when he has fulfilled the days, then to give place to another in the service. But when he turns again to the human mode of life, let it be permitted him both to go to a friend's house and, when invited, to attend a banquet, not of all men, but of the best; and at such a time it is not amiss to go into the marketplace now and then, and to greet a governor or the ruler of a province, and to help, so far as is fitting, those who reasonably ask his aid.
To Zeno

Many other things bear witness to you that you stand among the first in the art of medicine, and that in character and reasonableness and the temperance of your life you are in harmony with your art; but now the chief witness has been added: though absent, you draw the city of the Alexandrians to yourself; so great a sting, like a bee, have you left behind in her. And rightly so; for well does it seem to be said by Homer too: "One man that is a physician is worth many other men." But you are not simply a physician, but a teacher also of the art to those who wish it, so that, what physicians are to the multitude, that you are to them. The very cause of your exile sets you free from it, and that most splendidly. For if it was on account of Georgius that you were removed from Alexandria, you were removed unjustly, and most justly may you return again. Come back, then, with full honour and your former rank, and let there be laid up a common favour to us from both parties, restoring to the Alexandrians Zeno, and to you Alexandria.

It is fitting, I think, that the priests, when they are ministering within, should wear the most magnificent attire, but outside the temples the ordinary dress, without extravagance. For it is not reasonable to abuse the things given us for the honour of the gods into vainglory and empty conceit. Therefore we must abstain in the marketplace from costlier dress and from display, and in a word from all ostentation. The gods, indeed, admiring so greatly the self-control of Amphiaraus, since they had decreed the destruction of that army with which, knowing it, he yet marched, and the doom was therefore unavoidable for him, made him a different man from what he had been and removed him to a divine portion. Of all those who marched against Thebes, who painted devices upon their shields before they had accomplished anything and raised their trophies in anticipation of the disaster of the Cadmeians, this companion of the gods marched with arms that bore no device, and his gentleness and self-control were attested even by his enemies. Therefore I think we priests too must be temperate in the matter of our attire, that we may find the gods gracious; since it is no small offence against them when we make our sacred garments common and public, and offer them simply for men to gaze at, as though they were some marvel. For if this happens, many who are not pure draw near to us, and through this the symbols of the gods are defiled. And how great is the lawlessness and contempt toward the gods, when we ourselves, not living in priestly fashion, wear the dress of priests! But concerning these matters too we shall speak elsewhere with precision; for the present I write of them to you only in outline.
To the high priest Theodorus

. . . is it not right to grant to men this very thing which belongs to inanimate timbers? For suppose that a man has obtained a priesthood and chances to be unworthy of it: ought we not to forbear so long, until, having recognised that he is wicked and having barred him from his service, we make the name of priest, that was perhaps rashly conferred, accountable to insult and chastisement and penalty? If you do not know these things, you seem to know nothing else of what is moderate. For what experience have you of justice at all, who do not know what is a priest and what a private man? And where is your share of self-control, you who maltreated this man, before whom you ought even to have risen from your seat? Which is the most shameful thing of all, and especially in you, having no excuse either toward gods or toward men. The bishops and elders of the Galilaeans, it may be, sit with you, if not in public, because of me, yet privately and in your house; but because of you the priest has been beaten; for otherwise the high priest among you would never by Zeus have come to this petition. But since the things in Homer seem to you mere fable, hearken to the oracles of the lord of Didyma, that you may see how of old he admonished the Hellenes well by deed, and how later he taught by words those who were not temperate: "All those who against the priests, in the wantonness of their minds, work folly against the immortals, and against their honours plot opposition with thoughts that fear not the gods, shall not pass through to the end the whole path of life, all those who have done outrage to the blessed gods, whose god-revered ministering honour those men have taken away." The god, then, declares that not those who strike or insult, but those who deprive the priests of their honours, are enemies of the gods; and he who strikes one would be a temple-robber. I, therefore, since by ancestral right I am supreme high priest, and have now obtained also the office of prophet of Apollo of Didyma, forbid you for three courses of the moon to trouble the priest in any matter; and if in this time you shall appear worthy, when the high priest of the city writes to me whether you are acceptable to us, I will then take counsel with the gods concerning you afterward. This penalty I lay upon you for your rashness. As for the curses from the gods, the men of old were wont to utter and write them; yet it does not seem to me to be well. For nowhere do the gods themselves appear to have done such a thing. And besides, we ought to be ministers of prayers. Wherefore I think it well, and I join in praying with you, that, having earnestly entreated the gods, you may obtain forgiveness for your offences.

To these licentious theatres let no one of the priests anywhere resort, nor bring an actor into his own house; for it in no way befits him. And if it were possible to drive these things out of the theatres altogether, so as to give them back, purified, to Dionysus, I should certainly have tried eagerly to bring it about. But as it is, thinking this neither possible nor, even if it should prove possible, expedient, I have wholly refrained from this ambition; but I require the priests to withdraw and stand apart from the licentiousness of the theatres, leaving it to the people. Let no priest, then, enter a theatre, nor have for friend an actor or a charioteer, nor let any dancer or mime come to his door. To the sacred contests I permit to resort only whoever wishes, that is, those from which women are forbidden to take part not in the competition only but even in the spectacle. As for the hunting-shows, what need is there to speak, all those that are held within the theatres in the cities, that priests not only, but even the children of priests, must abstain from them?
To Theodorus, concerning Pegasius

We should never readily have admitted Pegasius, had we not been clearly persuaded that, even before, while he seemed to be a bishop of the Galilaeans, he knew how to revere and honour the gods. I do not report this to you on hearsay from those who are wont to speak according to enmity or friendship, since indeed such things about him had been much dinned even into my own ears, and, by the gods, I thought I ought to hate him as I hated none of the basest of men. But when, having been summoned to the camp by the late Constantius, I was journeying by this road, having risen at deep dawn I came from the Troad to Ilion about the time when the marketplace fills. And he came to meet me, and, when I wished to view the city—for this was my pretext for visiting the temples—he became my guide and showed me everywhere.

Now it would perhaps have been well to have said this before the rest, from what source and how the priests ought to be appointed; but it is no absurdity that my discourse should end with this. I say that the best men in the cities are to be appointed, and especially those most devoted to the gods, and next those most loving toward men, whether they be poor or rich; and in this matter let there be no distinction at all between obscure and distinguished; for he who through modesty has remained unnoticed ought not, because of the obscurity of his rank, to be barred. Even if a man be a poor commoner, if he have in himself these two things, love of the gods and love of man, let him be appointed priest. And a proof of love of the gods is if he has brought all his household to piety toward the gods; a proof of love of man, if even out of little he readily shares with those in need and gives gladly, trying to do good to as many as he is able.
To Theodorus

I have composed for you a kind of letter more peculiar than for the others, because you have a greater share of friendship toward me than, I think, the others have. For our common guide is no small bond, and you doubtless remember it. It is no short time since, while I was still spending my days in the West, having learned that you were greatly pleasing to him, I counted you a friend; though it has been my wont, through excessive caution, to regard that saying as well said: "For I never met him nor saw him," and to hold that knowledge must come before friendship, and trial before knowledge. But there was, it seems, no small weight with me also in the words "He himself has said it." Therefore both then I thought I must enrol you among my acquaintance, and now I entrust to you a matter dear to me and most profitable to all men everywhere. And if you administer it well, as it is right to hope, know that you will furnish great gladness here, and a good hope, a greater one, for the time to come. For neither are we among those who are persuaded that souls either perish before their bodies or perish together with them; and we believe no man, but the gods alone, who alone are likely to know these things best, if indeed it is fitting to call "likely" what is necessary; since it befits men to conjecture about such matters, but it is necessary that the gods should know them with certainty.

For we must give special attention to this part, and from it must our cure proceed. For since, I think, it came about that the poor were neglected and overlooked by the priests, the impious Galilaeans observed this and devoted themselves to this kind of philanthropy, and through what looks like a good work they confirmed their worst deeds. For just as those who lure children with a cake, by throwing it to them twice and three times, persuade them to follow, and then, when they have drawn them far from their homes, put them aboard a ship and sell them, and what for a little while seemed sweet became bitter for all the rest of life, so these too, beginning in the same way with what they call their love-feast and hospitality and service of tables, for the thing, like the name, is much used among them, have led very many into atheism. . . .
To the Alexandrians

If you do not reverence Alexander your founder, and before him the great god, the most holy Sarapis, how is it that no thought even of the common humanity and decency came into your minds? And I will add, of us also, whom all the gods, and first of all the great Sarapis, thought fit to set over the inhabited world; to whom it belonged to keep for ourselves the judgement concerning those who had wronged you. But anger, perhaps, and rage deceived you, which is wont to do dreadful things, dislodging the wits; for you, having checked the first rush of your passion, afterward added lawlessness to your well-considered first resolve, and were not ashamed, being a people, to dare the very things for which you justly hated those men. Tell me, in the name of Sarapis, for what wrongs were you angry with Georgius? You will say, doubtless, that the late Constantius exasperated him against you, and then he brought an army into the holy city, and the general of Egypt seized the most holy precinct of the god, plundering thence images and votive offerings and the adornment within the temples. And when you, naturally indignant, tried to defend the god, or rather the possessions of the god, he dared to send the soldiers against you unjustly and lawlessly and impiously, fearing Georgius, perhaps, more than Constantius, who watched him narrowly to see whether he would deal with you in a more moderate and statesmanlike, rather than tyrannical, fashion. Being angry, then, for these things with Georgius the enemy of the gods, you again defiled the holy city, when you might have subjected him to the votes of the judges. For thus the deed would have been no murder nor lawlessness, but a fitting justice, keeping you wholly guiltless, punishing him who had committed incurable impiety, and chastening all others who hold the gods in light esteem and who, moreover, count such cities and flourishing peoples as nothing, but make cruelty against them a mere by-work of their own power.
To Arsacius, high priest of Galatia

Hellenism does not yet prosper as we would, by reason of those who profess it; but the things of the gods are splendid and great, beyond all prayer and all hope. May Adrasteia be gracious to our words; for so great and so swift a change, in so short a time, none would have dared even to pray for a little while ago. Why, then, do we think these things suffice, and do not consider how greatly atheism has been advanced by kindness toward strangers, and care for the burial of the dead, and the pretended holiness of life? Each of these, I think, ought to be truly practised by us. And it is not enough that you alone be such, but all the priests throughout Galatia without exception; whom either put to shame or persuade to be earnest, or remove from the priestly service, if they do not, together with their wives and children and servants, draw near to the gods, but suffer their household, or sons, or wives to be impious toward the gods, preferring atheism to god-fearing. Next, exhort the priest neither to frequent the theatre, nor to drink in a tavern, nor to be patron of any base or disgraceful trade or occupation; and honour those who obey, but thrust out those who disobey. Establish in each city frequent hostels, that strangers may enjoy our kindness, not our own people only, but also any other who is in need of money. As for the source from which you shall provide this, I have already devised a plan. For I have ordered that every year throughout all Galatia thirty thousand bushels of corn and sixty thousand measures of wine be given; the fifth part of which I say must be spent upon the poor who serve the priests, and the rest distributed by us to strangers and beggars. For it is shameful that, while no Jew ever begs, and the impious Galilaeans support not only their own poor but ours as well, our own people should be seen to lack our aid. Teach also those who hold to Hellenism to contribute to such services, and the Hellenic villages to offer their first-fruits to the gods; and accustom those of the Hellenic faith to such good works, teaching them that this was of old our practice. Homer, at any rate, made Eumaeus say: "Stranger, it is not lawful for me, even if a worse man than you should come, to dishonour a stranger; for from Zeus come all strangers and beggars; and a gift, though small, is welcome." Let us not, then, by allowing others to outdo us in the good deeds that are properly our own, ourselves disgrace, or rather betray, by our slothfulness, our reverence toward the gods. If I learn that you are doing these things, I shall be full of gladness.
To Ecdicius, prefect of Egypt

Some men have a passion for horses, others for birds, others for wild beasts; but in me, from childhood, there has been a strong longing for the acquisition of books. It would therefore be absurd if I should suffer these to be appropriated by men for whom gold alone does not suffice to glut their great love of wealth, and who, besides, are minded to filch these too without scruple. Grant me, then, this favour as to a private man: that all the books of Georgius be found out. For he had many philosophical works, many rhetorical, and many also of the teaching of the impious Galilaeans; which last I should wish to have utterly destroyed, but, lest the more useful be carried off together with these, let all of them too be sought out with care. Let the secretary of Georgius be your guide in this search, who, if he tracks them down faithfully, may know that he will obtain freedom as his reward; but if he prove in any way a knave in the matter, he shall be brought to the test of torture. I myself know the books of Georgius, if not all, yet many; for he lent me some, while I was in Cappadocia, to copy, and received them back again.
An edict concerning Athanasius

He who has been expelled by very many royal and imperial commands ought to have waited for at least one imperial command before returning to his own country, and not, using audacity and recklessness, have insulted the laws as though they did not exist; since indeed even now to the Galilaeans who were banished by the late Constantius we have granted not a return to their churches, but a return to their own countries. But I learn that the most audacious Athanasius, lifted up by his accustomed insolence, has again seized what among them is called the episcopal throne; and that this is no small offence to the god-fearing people of the Alexandrians. Wherefore we proclaim to him to depart from the city, from whatever day he receives the letters of our clemency, forthwith; but if he remains within the city we proclaim against him far greater and harsher punishments.
To Evagrius

A little property of four fields, given to me by my grandmother in Bithynia, I give as a gift to your disposal—too little to enrich a man greatly or make him wealthy, yet not, even so, a wholly unpleasing gift, if I should describe its particulars to you. And there is nothing to forbid me to jest with you, who are full of graces and good taste. It is distant from the sea not more than twenty stades, and no merchant nor sailor, prating and insolent, disturbs the place. Yet it is not wholly bereft of the gifts of Nereus, for it has always fish fresh and still gasping; and, going up to a little hill that rises from the buildings, you will see the sea, the Propontis, and the islands, and the city named after the noble emperor, not standing among seaweed and moss, nor vexed by the unpleasant and unnameable refuse cast up upon the beaches and the sands, but among smilax and thyme and fragrant grass. There is great quiet as you lie down and look into a book, and then, resting your eyes, it is most pleasant to gaze out upon the ships and the sea. This, when I was quite a young lad, seemed to me a most dear summer retreat; for it has also springs not poor, and a bath not unlovely, and a garden and trees. And being now a man, I longed for that old way of life, and came there often, and our meeting was not without discourse. There is here too a small memorial of my husbandry, a little vineyard, bearing wine fragrant and sweet, which does not wait to receive anything from time. You shall see Dionysus and the Graces. The cluster, both on the vine and crushed in the press, breathes of roses, and the new must in the jars is already a fragment of nectar, if we believe Homer. Why, then, has not such a vine become great, nor spread over very many plethra? Perhaps I have not been an eager husbandman; but since for me the bowl of Dionysus is sober and needs much water from the nymphs, I have provided only so much as suffices for myself and my friends, who are a small company. This now I give you as a gift, dear friend, small indeed as it is, but a graceful one, from friend to friend, "from home to home," as the wise poet Pindar says. I have written this letter hurriedly, by lamplight, so that, if anything is amiss in it, do not examine it sharply, nor as one orator another.
To Themistius the philosopher

The proverb says: "You announce no war"; and I would add, from the comedy: "O you that announce a treasure of words." Come, then, prove it by deeds, and hasten to me; for you will come as friend to friend. The common and constant business of affairs seems indeed somewhat burdensome to those who do not make it a by-work; but those who share the care of it are, as I am persuaded, reasonable men, and intelligent, and altogether competent for everything. They give me, therefore, ease, so that I may rest without neglecting anything; for we are together with one another not with the dissembling of courts—of which alone, I suppose, you have hitherto had experience—wherein men, while they praise, hate with a hatred such as they bear not even to their bitterest enemies, but with the freedom that befits us, refuting one another when there is need and reproving, we love one another no less than the closest comrades. Hence it is possible for us—and far be envy—to be earnest in our leisure, and not to be worn out in our earnestness, and to sleep without fear. For even when I am awake, I am awake not on my own behalf rather than on behalf of all the rest, as is fitting.
To the people of some city, remitting their debts

To a king who looked to gain, your request would have appeared a hard one, and he would not have thought it right to harm the public revenue by a private favour to certain men; but since we have made it our aim not to gather the most we can from our subjects, but to be the authors of the most good to them, this very thing shall release you from your debts. It shall release you, however, not from all of them simply, but the matter shall be divided, part to you and part to the needs of the soldiers, from which you yourselves, of course, reap no small benefit, namely peace and security. Therefore up to the third indiction we remit to you all that is owing from the time now past; but after this you shall pay according to custom. For both to you the remission is favour enough, and we must not neglect the common interest. Concerning this I have written also to the prefects, that the favour may pass into effect for you. May the gods preserve you in health for all time.
To the Thracians (or a letter on behalf of the Argives)

On behalf of the city of the Argives one might say much, were he minded to glorify her, both old things and new. For of the Trojan war, as later of the Persian war for the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, the greater part of the work belongs to them. Both, indeed, seem to have been done in common by Hellas; but it is right that, as in the toils and the care, so also in the praises, the leaders should have the greater share. But these things seem somewhat ancient; while what came after them—the return of the Heracleidae, and how the privilege was set apart for the eldest, and the colony sent thence to the Macedonians, and that, dwelling so close beside the Lacedaemonians, the city kept itself ever unenslaved and free—was the work of no small or common courage. And as for those great things done against the Persians by the Macedonians, one might justly suppose that they belong to this city; for Philip and Alexander, of those most famous among the ancestors, this was their fatherland. Later, to the Romans she submitted, not so much conquered as in alliance, and shared, I suppose, like the rest, in freedom and in the other rights which the rulers for the time being grant to the cities of Hellas.
To the priest Theodorus

If I make light of your letters, then "afterward the gods themselves destroyed my wits." For what good thing is not in your letters? Goodwill, faithfulness, truth, and, before these, that without which the rest are nothing, prudence, displayed in all her parts—in quickness of mind, in understanding, in good counsel. As for my not answering—for this too you blamed me—I have no leisure, by the gods; and do not think that the matter is affectation or play. I call the gods of eloquence to witness that, except Homer and Plato, no book follows me, neither philosophic nor rhetorical nor grammatical, nor any history of those in common use; and even these very ones are like amulets and charms, for they are ever bound to me. Of the rest I have but few, and I pray, though needing them, as is natural, if ever at any other time, then now, very many and great prayers. But affairs press me, hemmed in on every side; and you yourself will perhaps see, when I am come into Syria.
To Maximus the philosopher (or to Philip)

I, by the gods, while still Caesar, wrote to you, and, I think, more than once. I often set out to do so, but was hindered, now by one cause, now by another, and then by the wolf-friendship that arose, after my proclamation, between me and the late Constantius; for I was altogether careful not to write to anyone beyond the Alps, lest I should bring upon him grievous troubles. Take it, then, as a proof of my goodwill that I did not write; for the tongue is often unwilling to agree with the mind. And perhaps there is something for the vulgar to plume and boast themselves upon in the display of imperial letters, when, like rings carried about by men of no taste, they are paraded before the unaccustomed. But true friendship comes chiefly through likeness, and in the second place when a man admires truly and not in pretence, and when the gentle and moderate and self-controlled is loved by one who is, by fortune and understanding, his superior. These little notes are full of much vanity and much trifling; and I often blame myself for making them too long and being too talkative, when I might teach my tongue Pythagorean silence.
To Eustochius

That the science of medicine is salutary to men, the plain evidence of its usefulness bears witness. Wherefore the sons of the philosophers rightly proclaim that it too came down from heaven; for the weakness of our nature, and the maladies that befall us, are set right by it. Therefore, according to the reckoning of justice, in harmony with the kings on high who so decreed, we, of our clemency, order that you be allowed to pass the rest of your time undisturbed by the burdens of public service.
To Theodora

The book which you sent by Mygdonius we have received, and all the tokens besides that were sent to us during the festival. Each of these is pleasant to me; but pleasanter than all, be assured, was to learn concerning your goodness that, by the gods' grace, your body is in health, and that the things concerning the gods are pursued by you more carefully and more earnestly. As to what you wrote to the philosopher Maximus, that my friend Seleucus is at variance with you, be persuaded that he does and says nothing of the kind before me, by which he might most slander you; on the contrary, he says nothing but good of you, and I do not yet say that he is even well disposed toward you—for that he himself must know, and the gods who see all things. But that, before me, he abstains from all such things, I say with strict truth. It seems to me, therefore, ridiculous to consider not what is done by him but what is hidden, and to examine things of which I have no plain proof. But since you ran him down at great length, and revealed also something about yourself, making plain to me the cause of your enmity toward him, this much I say to you frankly: that if you love anyone, man or woman, slave or free, who neither now worships the gods nor whom you have any hope of persuading, you do wrong. For consider, first in your own case: if one of the servants you love should take part with those who revile and blaspheme you, and serve them rather, and turn away from and loathe us, your friends, would you not wish him to perish at once, or rather would you not yourself punish him? What then? Are the gods of less honour than friends? Reckon this too in their case, holding them as masters and us as their slaves. If, then, one of us, who say we are servants of the gods, should cherish a servant who loathes them and turns away from their worship, is it not just either to persuade and save him, or to put him out of the house and sell him, if one cannot easily despise the loss of a slave? But I would not consent to be loved by those who do not love the gods; and this I say that you, and all who lay claim to priestly functions, ought, having now thought of it, to lay hold the more earnestly of holiness toward the gods; and the priest ought to furnish from his own house a reasonable reverence, and to show it whole and pure throughout from such maladies, first of all.
To Theodora

All the books sent by you I have gladly received, and your letters, by the excellent Mygdonius. And scarcely having leisure, as the gods know—I say it without affectation—I have written this reply to you. May you fare well, and write me always such things.
To a priestess

I have received all that your wisdom sent, the good and fair tidings and gifts from the gods; and having confessed great thanks to the heavenly gods, in the second place I have rendered thanks to your magnanimity, that you are eager above all to entreat the gods on our behalf, and are zealous to make known to us speedily the good things that have appeared to you.
To Aristoxenus the philosopher

Ought one to wait for an invitation, and never to value coming uninvited? But take care lest we introduce a hard rule of law, if from friends one must wait for the same things as from acquaintances who are simply and casually known. Here someone will be at a loss: how are we friends, who have not seen one another? And how friends with those who lived a thousand years ago, yes, by Zeus, and two thousand? Because they were all earnest and noble and good in character. And we too desire to be such, though in being so, as far as I am concerned, we fall very far short. Yet the desire at least ranks us in some sort in the same class with them. But why do I prate longer about this? For whether one must come uninvited, you will doubtless come; or whether you wait for an invitation, behold, here too an invitation comes to you from us. Meet me, then, near Tyana, in the name of Zeus the god of friendship, and show me a man who in Cappadocia is purely a Hellene. For so far I see men who are unwilling to sacrifice, and a few who are willing but do not know how.
An edict concerning teachers

Right education, we hold, is not that elegance of words and tongue which is laboured over, but a sound disposition of a mind that has understanding, and true opinions concerning things good and evil, noble and base. Whoever, then, thinks one thing and teaches another to those who come to him, seems to fall as far short of being educated as he falls short of being a good man. And if in small matters the difference between thought and tongue be slight, it is an evil, yet somehow tolerable; but if in the greatest matters a man thinks one thing and teaches the contrary of what he thinks, how is not this the very mark of hucksters, and not of honest men, but of utterly worthless men, who praise most what they think most worthless, deceiving and luring by their praises those into whom, I think, they wish to transfer their own evils? All, then, who profess to teach anything ought to be reasonable in character, and not to carry in their souls opinions at variance with what they publicly handle. But far more than all, I think, ought those to be such who associate with the young in the matter of letters, becoming interpreters of the ancient writers, whether rhetoricians or grammarians, and still more the sophists. For these wish to be teachers not of words only but of morals, and they claim that political philosophy is their own province. Whether this be true or not, let it pass for the present. But, while praising them for reaching after such fair professions, I should praise them still more if they would not lie, nor convict themselves of thinking one thing and teaching their pupils another. What then? Were not Homer, and Hesiod, and Demosthenes, and Herodotus, and Thucydides, and Isocrates, and Lysias led in all their learning by the gods? Did not some of them hold themselves sacred to Hermes, and others to the Muses? It is absurd, I think, that those who expound their works should dishonour the gods whom those men honoured. Yet, though I think this absurd, I do not say that they must change their views and so associate with the young; I give them the choice, either not to teach what they do not deem worthy, or, if they wish to teach, first to persuade their pupils in deed that neither Homer nor Hesiod nor any of these whom they expound, and of whom they have condemned impiety, folly, and error concerning the gods, is really such as they say. For since they are nourished and earn their pay from the writings of these men, they confess themselves most basely greedy of gain, and ready to endure anything for a few drachmas. Now until this time there were many reasons for not frequenting the temples, and the fear that hung over us on every side gave excuse for hiding the truest opinions about the gods; but since the gods have given us liberty, it seems to me absurd that men should teach others what they do not deem to be good. But if they think those wise of whom they are the interpreters, and before whom they sit as prophets, let them first emulate their piety toward the gods; but if they suppose those men to have erred concerning the most honoured beings, then let them go into the churches of the Galilaeans to expound Matthew and Luke, in obedience to whom you ordain abstinence from sacrifices. I would that your ears and your tongues might be born anew, as you would say, into those things in which may I ever have part, and whoever thinks and acts dear to me. For teachers and masters let this common law be laid down; but whoever of the young wishes to attend is not barred. For neither is it reasonable to shut out from the best road the boys who do not yet know which way to turn, and to lead them by fear, against their will, to the rites of their fathers. And yet it were just, as we heal the frenzied against their will, so to heal these too against their will; only let pardon be granted to all for such a disease. For we ought, I think, to teach, and not to chastise, the foolish.
To Atarbius

I, by the gods, do not wish the Galilaeans to be slain, nor beaten contrary to justice, nor to suffer any other evil; yet I say that the god-fearing must by all means be preferred. For through the folly of the Galilaeans almost everything has been overturned, while through the goodwill of the gods we are all preserved. Therefore we must honour the gods and the god-fearing, both men and cities.
To Porphyrius

There was a very large and great library of Georgius, of philosophers of every kind, of many commentators, and not least among them many and various books of the Galilaeans. Seek out, then, this whole library all together, and take care to send it to Antioch, knowing that you yourself will be visited with the heaviest penalty, unless you track it down with all diligence, and, by every kind of proof and by oaths of every sort, and, more, by the torture of the slaves, compel those who are in any way suspected of having stolen the books—if you cannot persuade them—to bring everything forth into the open. Farewell.
To the Byzacians

We have restored to you all the senators, and the sons of senators, whether they gave themselves over to the superstition of the Galilaeans, or in some other way contrived to escape the council, except those who have already performed public services in the metropolis.
To Hecebolius

I have treated all the Galilaeans so gently and humanely that no one anywhere suffers violence, nor is dragged to a temple, nor is wronged in any other such matter against his own purpose. But the people of the Arian church, waxing wanton through their wealth, attacked the followers of Valentinus, and dared at Edessa such things as could never happen in a well-governed city. Therefore, since by their most admirable law they have been bidden to sell their goods and give to the poor, that they may go the more easily into the kingdom of heaven, we, helping the men of their church toward this end, have ordered that all the money of the church of the Edessenes be taken up to be given to the soldiers, and that its properties be added to our privy purse; that, being poor, they may be temperate, and may not be deprived of that heavenly kingdom for which they still hope. And to the inhabitants of Edessa we proclaim that they abstain from all faction and strife, lest, having stirred up our humanity, you pay the penalty, on your own heads, for the disorder of the commonwealth, being punished with sword and exile and fire.
To the Bostrenes

I thought that the leaders of the Galilaeans would feel greater gratitude to me than to him who governed the empire before me. For under him it befell most of them to be banished and persecuted and imprisoned, and already great numbers of those whom they call heretics had been slaughtered, as at Samosata and Cyzicus and in Paphlagonia and Bithynia and Galatia, and in many other nations whole villages were utterly destroyed and laid waste; but under me the contrary. For those who were exiled have been set free, and those whose goods were confiscated have received back, by law from us, all their own. Yet they have come to such a pitch of raving madness and folly that, because they are not allowed to play the tyrant, nor to do what they once did to one another, and afterward to us the god-fearing, being provoked, they leave no stone unturned, and dare to throw the multitudes into confusion and to raise sedition, being impious toward the gods and disobedient to our commands, humane though these are. For we suffer none of them to be dragged unwilling to the altars, and we expressly proclaim to them that, if any willingly wishes to share with us in the lustral water and the libations, he must first offer purifying sacrifices and entreat the averting gods. So far are we from wishing or designing that any of the impious should ever share in our holy sacrifices, until he has purified his soul by prayers to the gods and his body by the lawful purifications.
To Callixene

Time alone reveals the just man, as we have learned from those of old; but I would say that it reveals the pious man too and the lover of the gods. "But Penelope also," you will say, "was attested to be a lover of her husband." Then who, after love of her husband, sets in second place in a woman the love of the gods, and does not appear to have drunk much mandragora? And if one takes into account the times also, and that Penelope was praised by well-nigh all for her love of her husband, while a little while ago pious women were in danger, and, to add to the evils, that the time was twice as long, is it possible for you fittingly to be set beside Penelope? But do not make small your praises, in return for which all the gods will reward you, while we for our part will honour you with a double priesthood. For in addition to the one you held before, of the most holy goddess Demeter, we entrust to you the priesthood of the great Mother of the gods, the Phrygian, in god-beloved Pessinus.
To the philosopher Maximus (an invitation)

May the proem be not too commonplace: "The noble man." What follows you doubtless know. Indeed you have it; for you know, being a man of letters and a philosopher, what follows it, and you have me for a friend, if at least we are both noble men. For of you I would even contend that you are such; but of myself I am silent; may it be that others perceive me too to be such. But why, as if I were going to say something strange, do I go round in a circle when I should speak plainly? Come, and hasten, and, as the saying is, fly. A gracious god shall speed you on your way, with the Maiden of the Crossways; and the public post shall serve you, with a carriage if you wish to use one, and two spare horses.
To a physician

"One must love a guest while he is present, and send him on when he wishes to go": so the wise Homer laid down the law. But between us there is something better than the friendship of guest and host, both through such culture as we have and through reverence toward the gods; so that no one would justly charge me with transgressing the law of Homer, even though I judged it right for you to stay longer with us. But, seeing that your poor body needs more care, I have allowed you to go to your own country, and have taken thought for the ease of your journey. You may use, then, a public carriage; and may all the gods, with Asclepius, escort you on your way, and grant that we meet again.
To a leader of the people

The proverb says: "Do you tell me my dream"; and I seem to be telling you your waking vision. The Nile, they say, lifted high in its cubits, has filled all Egypt; and if you long to hear the number too, by the twentieth of September it rose fifteen cubits. This Theophilus the commander reports. If, then, you did not know it, hear it from us and rejoice.
To Ecdicius, prefect of Egypt

Even if for other reasons you do not write to us, at least concerning Athanasius, the enemy of the gods, you ought to have written, especially since you have long known what we have rightly resolved. I swear by the great Sarapis that, if the enemy of the gods, Athanasius, does not leave that city before the Kalends of December, or rather all Egypt, I shall fine the officials under your charge a hundred pounds of gold. And you know how slow I am to condemn, but far slower, having once condemned, to relent. And in his own hand: It vexes me much to be despised. By all the gods, there is nothing I would so gladly see, or rather hear, done by you, as that Athanasius be driven beyond the borders of Egypt—the abominable man, who under my reign dared to baptise Greek women of rank. Let him be driven out.
To the Alexandrians

If any of the Galilaeans had been your founder—men who, having transgressed their own law, paid such penalties as were fitting, having chosen to live lawlessly and brought in a new preaching and a recent teaching—even so there would have been no reason for Athanasius to be sought after by you. But as it is, since Alexander is the founder of the city, and your guardian god is King Sarapis, together with the Maiden who sits beside him and the queen of all Egypt, Isis . . . You do not emulate the city in her health, but the diseased part dares to claim for itself the name of the city.
To the Alexandrians

I hear that there is among you an obelisk of stone, raised to a sufficient height, but lying cast away upon the shore as though it were some most worthless thing. For this the late Constantius had a ship built, to convey it to my fatherland, the city of Constantine. But since it has befallen him, the gods willing, to go from here to there the appointed journey, the city demands of me the offering, being my fatherland and belonging to me more than to him. For he loved her as a sister, but I as a mother; for I was born there and reared there, and I cannot be ungrateful toward her. What then? Since I love you no less than my fatherland, I grant that there be set up among you also the bronze image. For there has lately been made a statue of colossal size, which, when you have set it up, you shall have in place of the stone offering a bronze image of a man whom, you say, you long for, a likeness and a form, instead of a four-cornered stone bearing Egyptian carvings. And the report, too, that there are some who tend it and sleep at its peak quite persuades me that for the sake of this superstition I ought to remove it. For those who behold the men who sleep there—since there is, as it chances, much filth and much licentiousness about the place—neither believe it to be divine, and, through the superstition of those who attend it, become the more unbelieving toward the gods. For this very reason it is the more fitting that you should lend a hand and send it to my fatherland, which entertains you well when you sail into the Pontus, and that you should contribute, as it were, to her sustenance and her outward adornment. Surely it will be no ungrateful thing that something of yours should stand among them too, upon which, as you sail in toward the city, you may gaze with gladness.
To Ecdicius, prefect of Egypt

It is worth while, if anything is, to take thought also for sacred music. Choosing, then, from the people of the Alexandrians well-born youths, order that two artabae of corn be furnished to each of them monthly, and oil and wine besides; and clothing shall be provided by the overseers of the treasury. For the present let these be enrolled by voice. And if any are able to attain to the height of the science itself, let them know that very great prizes for their labour are laid up with us also. For that they themselves, before us, having had their souls purified by the divine music, will be the gainers, we must believe those who have rightly declared this before. So much, then, for the boys. As for those who are now studying under the musician Dioscorus, make them lay hold of the art more eagerly, since we are ready to aid them in whatever they wish.
To Nilus, surnamed Dionysius

You were better when you kept silence before than now when you defend yourself; for you did not revile me then, though perhaps you meant to; but now, as though in travail, you have poured out all at once your abuse against me. Or must I not count it both reviling and slander, that you supposed me like your own friends, to each of whom you offered yourself uninvited—or rather, to the first uninvited, but to the second, who only hinted that he wished to take you for an ally, you submitted? But whether I am like Constans and Magnentius, the deed itself, as the saying is, will show; while you, that you praise yourself, like Astydamas, after the comic poet—"O woman," as he says—is plain from what you wrote. For your fearlessness and your great boldness, and your "Would that you knew how great and what manner of man I am," and, in a word, all such things—bah!—how great a din and clatter of words it is! But, by the Graces and by Aphrodite, if you are so bold and noble, why did you take heed not to give offence a third time, if you must? For those who incur the hatred of rulers are, in the lightest and, one might say, the pleasantest case—at least for a man of sense—quickly freed from their troubles; but if a small further penalty is exacted, they suffer in their property; and the chief part of their anger, and to suffer, as they say, the irreparable, is to give up life. Despising all this, since you have come to know the private man and the man in his common and general nature, who is unknown to us late-learners, why then, in the name of the gods, did you say you took care not to give offence a third time? For surely I shall not, by being angry, make you wicked instead of good; for he would be a man to envy who in justice could do this; since, as Plato says, he could do the contrary also. But, virtue being its own master, you ought to have reckoned none of these things. But you think it a great matter to slander everyone, and to revile all without distinction, and to make the sanctuary of peace a workshop of war. Or do you think by this to defend your old faults before all men, and to make your present courage a screen for the cowardice you once showed? You have heard the fable of Babrius: "A weasel once fell in love with a comely man." The rest learn from the book. By saying much you would persuade no man that you have not become what you are, and what many men of old knew you to be. Your present ignorance and boldness, by the gods, philosophy did not implant in you; rather, on the contrary, that double ignorance of which Plato speaks. For, since you are in danger of knowing nothing—as neither do we—you think yourself the wisest of all, not of those now living only, but of those who have been, and perhaps of those who shall be. So far, to a pitch of folly, has your conceit advanced.
To the community of the Jews

Very burdensome to you, in times past, has been the yoke of your servitude—that you were subjected to unannounced assessments, and forced to bring in an unspeakable amount of gold to the accounts of the treasury; of which I saw much with my own eyes, and learned more by finding the registers kept against you. And further, when another levy was about to be ordered against you, I prevented it, and forced the impiety of such ill report to stop there, and gave to the fire the registers kept against you that lay in my archives, that no one might any longer be able to hurl against you such a report of impiety. And of these things he who is worthy of memory, my brother Constantius, was not so much the cause to you as the men barbarous in mind and godless in soul who feasted at his table; whom I, having taken in my own hands, thrust into a pit and destroyed, so that not even a memory of their destruction is any longer borne among us. And, wishing you to fare yet better, I have exhorted my brother Iulus, your most reverend patriarch, that the levy called the apostolē among you be stopped, and that no one any longer be able to wrong your multitudes by such exactions of tribute; so that from every side you may have freedom from care under my reign, and, enjoying peace, may make still greater prayers for my reign to him who is the highest, the Creator God, who has thought fit to crown me with his undefiled right hand. For it is natural that those who are involved in any anxiety should be straitened in mind and not dare to lift up their hands in prayer so freely; but that those who are wholly free from care should rejoice with their whole soul and make supplicating worship for the kingdom to the greater, who is able to direct our reign to the fairest ends, as we purpose. This you ought to do, that I too, when I have set the Persian war in order, may rebuild with my own labours the holy city of Jerusalem, which for many years you have longed to see inhabited, and may settle it, and with you give glory there to the Highest.
To the philosopher Maximus (or to a friend)

Since you have forgotten your promise—for this is the third day now—and the philosopher Priscus himself has not come, but has sent word that he is still delayed, I remind you and demand the debt. It is a debt which, as you know, is easy for you to pay, and most pleasant for me to receive. Send, then, the discourse and the sacred counsel; but, in the name of Hermes and the Muses, quickly, since you must know that you have crushed me even in these three days, if the Sicilian poet speaks truly when he says that those who long grow old in a single day. And if this is so, as indeed it is, you have tripled my old age, my noble friend. This I have dictated to you in the midst of business; for I was not able to write, having my hand less practised than my tongue—though, indeed, my tongue too has become, through disuse, less practised and less articulate. Farewell, my most longed-for and most beloved brother.
To Maximus the philosopher (or to Libanius)

You have rendered to Aristophanes the rewards of his piety toward the gods and of his zeal toward yourself, having changed and transformed his former reproaches into good repute, not for the present only, but for the time to come; since the slander of Paulus and the verdict of so-and-so are not like the discourses written by you. For those were hated even while they flourished, and died out together with those who wrought them; but your discourses are now loved by the true Hellenes, and, unless I am wholly mistaken in right judgement, will be loved in the time to come. You shall learn, then, whether you have persuaded me, or rather changed my mind, concerning Aristophanes. That I do not think him a slave to pleasures and money, I confess. Why should I not yield to the most philosophic and most truth-loving of the orators? It follows that I be further questioned by you on this: why, then, do we not change his misfortunes to a better lot, and do away with the reproaches that have fallen upon him through his adversities? "Let us two go together," as the saying is, "you and I, and take counsel." And it is just that you should counsel me not only that we ought to aid a man who has honoured the gods without guile, but also in what manner we ought to do it. And yet this too you have hinted at, in a way. But it is perhaps better not to write about such things, but to discuss them with one another. Farewell, my most longed-for and most beloved brother.
To a man whom he made consul

Hesiod the wise thinks one should invite one's neighbours to the feasts, that they may share the joy, since they share also the grief and the anxiety whenever some unlooked-for trouble falls. But I say one must invite one's friends, not one's neighbours; and the reason is that a neighbour may be an enemy, but a friend an enemy no more than white can be black or hot cold. And that you are my friend, and have been so not now only but of old, and have continued well-disposed, even if there were no other proof, yet that we are so minded and disposed toward you would be a great sign of it. Come, then, and share the consulship yourself. The public post shall bring you, using one carriage and a spare horse. And if I must add a further prayer, we have called upon the god of the crossways to be gracious to you.
An edict concerning funerals

We ought, indeed, having considered the matter at home, to confirm by law what now seems good, and to take up again the ancient custom, which the men of old, who laid down the laws well, conceiving that there is a very great difference between life and death, deemed it fitting to mark each by its proper practices in our deeds. For death is a perpetual rest—and this, then, is the "brazen sleep" hymned by the poets—while life, on the contrary, holds many things painful and many pleasant, and our doing is now in one way, now better. Considering this, they ordained that the rites toward the departed be performed apart, and that the affairs of daily life be ordered apart. Moreover, they held the gods to be the beginning and end of all things, and they thought that, living, we are under the gods, and, departing, we go again to the gods. Now whether both belong to the same gods, or whether some govern the living and others the dead, it is perhaps not even worth while to make public. But if, just as the sun is the author of day and night, of winter and summer, by his going and coming, so too the eldest of the gods himself, into whom are all things and from whom are all things, has appointed rulers over the living and allotted lords over the dead, we ought to render to each what is fitting in turn, and to imitate, through our daily life, the ordering of the gods that is in the universe.
To Arsaces, satrap of Armenia (a forgery, but transmitted in the corpus)

Haste to the array of the enemy, Arsaces, swifter than a word, arming your right hand against the Persian madness. For our preparation and our zeal have determined upon one of two things: either to pay the debt of nature on the borders of the Parthians, having wrought the greatest deeds and disposed of our adversaries most terribly; or, having mastered them, the gods presiding over us, to return as glorious victors to our native land, having raised trophies over the enemy. Putting away, then, all sloth and trickery, and remembering the late Constantine, and the substance of the well-born that was lavished upon you and the barbarians of your kind by the most delicate and extravagant Constantius, think now of me—of Julian, the high priest, the Caesar, the Augustus, the servant of the gods and of Ares, the destroyer of the Franks and the barbarians, the liberator of the Gauls and the Italians. But if you should plan anything else—for I learn that you are crafty, and a bad soldier, and a braggart, as my present affairs show; for you try to keep hidden with you a certain enemy of the common good—for the present I postpone this, because of the fortune of war; for the alliance of the gods suffices us for the overthrow of the enemy. But if fate should decide otherwise—for the power of fate is the will of the gods—I shall bear it without fear and nobly. But know that you shall be a mere by-work of the Persian hand, your household joined to your ruin with all its kindred, and the rule of the Armenians; and the city of the Nisibenes shall share your misfortune, the heavenly gods having long ago foretold this to us.
To Libanius the sophist

I came as far as Litarbae—it is a village of Chalcis—and I fell in with a road that still had remnants of the winter quarters of Antioch. Part of it, I think, was marsh and part hill, but the whole was rough, and in the marsh lay stones thrown down as if on purpose, fitted together by no art, in the way men are wont in other cities, when they build up the highways, to lay much rubble instead of mortar, and to set the stones close together as in a wall. When, having crossed it with difficulty, I came to the first halting-place, it was about the ninth hour, and I received within the courtyard the greater part of your council. What we said to one another you have perhaps heard; and you may learn it from us too, if you hear us, the gods willing.
To Libanius

The fable makes the eagle, when he would test the genuineness of his young, carry them still unfledged toward the upper air and hold them up to the rays of the sun, becoming, as it were, with the god for witness, the father of a true nestling and disowning a spurious brood. So I put my words into your hands as into those of Hermes the eloquent. And if they endure your hearing, it is for you to judge of them, whether they can take wing toward others also; but if not, cast them away at random as alien to the Muses, or drown them in a river as spurious. Surely the Rhine too does no wrong to the Celts, who sinks the spurious infants beneath his eddies, a fitting avenger of an unchaste bed; but those he recognises to be of pure seed he buoys up above the water and gives back into the hands of the trembling mother, granting her the safety of her child as an incorruptible witness of a pure and blameless marriage.
To Libanius
