They say that Daedalus dared to do violence to nature by art, fashioning wings of wax for Icarus. As for him, even if I praise his art, I do not admire his judgement; for he alone endured to trust the safety of his child to wax that melts. But if it were lawful for me, as for that Teian lyric poet, to change the nature of birds, I should not fly toward Olympus, nor for any reproach of love, but to the very foot of your mountains, that I might enfold you, my care, as Sappho says. But since nature, having shut me in the chains of a human body, will not suffer me to spread my wings toward the upper air, I come to you with such wings as I have, the wings of words, and write, and am with you in the only way I can. Surely Homer too names them "winged" for no other reason than this, that they can range everywhere, like the swiftest of birds, darting wherever they will. Do you yourself write also, my friend; for yours, surely, is an equal, if not a greater, plumage of words, by which you can pass to your comrades and from every side gladden them as though present.
To Libanius

There is a fuller occasion of pleasure when one may greet one's friends through a familiar man, so that you may fit the image of your own soul not only to those to whom you write, but to those who meet him. This very thing I myself do. For sending to you Antiochus, the tutor of my children, I could not bear to leave you ungreeted; so that, if you long for anything of our affairs, you may learn it more intimately from him. And if you too care anything for your lovers—as I believe you do—you will show it by never failing to write while you are able.
To Libanius

For when were you ever parted from us, that we should write, or when do we not behold you, as though present, with the eyes of the soul? We who not only seem always to be with you and to converse with you, but, in the present concerns of those near you, take such care of them as is fitting, as though under your presence. But if you wish to be written to by us as one absent, take care lest you yourself, by your very wish to be written to, rather reveal that you seem to be absent from us; only, if it is dear to you, even to this we willingly consent. By all means, as the saying goes, "you will be driving a running horse to the plain" by your bidding. Come, then, and render us like for like, and at our counter-summons do not be slow in the constant exchange. And yet I, for my part, do not wish to disturb the zeal you spend on the common good; rather, the more I guard you in your hunting of noble things, the more I should seem not only to do no wrong, but to benefit the whole Hellenic cause together, when, like a noble hound, I let you, undisturbed, devote yourself with whole spirit to the tracks of letters. But if you have such swiftness to spare that you neither neglect your friends nor fall short of those pursuits, come, use your speed for both.
To Libanius

Pindar thinks the Muses are silvern, likening, as it were, the conspicuous and brilliant quality of their art to the brightness of the metal; while the wise Homer calls silver "gleaming," and names water "silvery," as though, with the pure rays of the sun, it sparkled with the very brightness of the image; and the fair Sappho says the moon is silvern, and that for this reason it hides the face of the other stars. So one might judge that silver befits the gods rather than gold; yet for men, since silver is more useful than gold and is more with them—not, like gold, hidden beneath the earth or fleeing their sight, but both fair to behold and better in daily use—this saying is not my own, but the saying of men of old. And if, in return for the gold coin you sent, we give you another of silver of equal value, do not judge the favour the less, nor think, as in the case of Glaucus, that the exchange is to the worse; since not even Diomede, perhaps, would have given silver for gold, seeing that the silver was far more useful than the other and knew how to turn aside spear-points as though they were lead. These things we play with you, taking from your own writing the lead for frankness toward you. But if you really wish to send us gifts more precious than gold, write, and do not cease doing this continually; for to me even a small letter from you is judged fairer than whatever good thing one might name.
To Libanius
I both write and claim to receive the like in return. But if I do wrong by writing continually, I ask to be wronged in turn by suffering the same.
To Libanius

There is even in a small letter a greater pleasure, when the goodwill of the writer is measured not by the smallness of the letter so much as by the greatness of his soul. And if now too the words of greeting from us have been brief, do not, even so, judge by them the longing they carry; but, knowing how far the love we bear toward you is stretched, grant pardon for the brevity of the letter, and be not slow to repay us in kind. For everything you give, even if it be small, preserves with us the mark of every good.
To Libanius

Let Echo be a goddess, as you say, and a chatterer, and, if you will, the consort of Pan too; for I shall not contend. For though Nature would teach me that Echo is the answering sound of a voice, struck back from the air to the hearing in the opposite direction, yet, obeying men of old and of recent times no less than your own argument, I am put to shame to deny that Echo is a goddess. What, then, would this be to us, if by a great measure we surpass Echo in our friendly offices toward you? For she answers not to all that she hears, but rather to the last of the voice, like a stingy beloved who returns the lover's kiss only with the tips of her lips; but we both begin gladly the offices toward you, and again, at your challenge, send back the like, as it were a ball. So you would not be beforehand in being yourself liable to what you write, and in ranking yourself—you who, receiving more, give back least—rather than us, who are eager to have the advantage on both sides, as like to the image you draw. Yet whether you give in equal measure to what you receive, or not, to us whatever it is permitted to receive from you is pleasant, and is believed to suffice for the whole.
To Libanius

"You have come, Telemachus," says the verse; and I have already seen you in your letters, and have taken the impress of the image of your sacred soul as on a small seal the stamp of a great character. For in a little space much may be shown; since Pheidias the wise was known not from the statue at Olympia or at Athens alone, but knew also how to enclose the work of great art in a small carving, such as they say his cicada was, and his bee, and, if you will, his fly too; of which each, though by nature it was wrought in bronze, was by his art given a soul. But in those works, perhaps, the very smallness of the creatures lent something fitting to his proportioned art; but do you, if you please, consider the Alexander hunting on horseback, whose whole measure is no greater than a fingernail. So is the marvel of the art poured over each, that Alexander already smites the beast and frightens the beholder, awing him through the whole figure, while the horse, balanced upon the very tips of his feet, escaping a fixed stand, is moved, by the stealthy artifice of energy, by the art itself. This very thing, my noble friend, you too do for us. For, as one already crowned often through the whole course in the lists of Hermes the eloquent, by what you write in a few words you display the height of your excellence, and in truth you rival the Odysseus of Homer, who, by saying only who he was, sufficed to amaze the Phaeacians. And if you need from us, too, something of the friendly smoke of your own kind, there is no grudging. Surely even from the weaker something good may come, as the mouse that saved the lion in the fable sufficiently shows.
To Eumenius and Pharianus

I was near to weeping; and yet I ought to have spoken well-omened words when I uttered your name. For I was reminded of our noble and wholly admirable father; and if you emulate him, you yourself will be happy, and will give to the world, as he did, something to take pride in; but if you are slothful, you will grieve me, and yourself you will blame when there is no longer any profit in it.
To Himerius

Not without tears did I read your letter, which you wrote upon the death of your wife, announcing the excess of your grief. For, besides that the event in itself is worthy of grief—that a wife young and chaste and dear to her husband, and besides the mother of holy children, should be snatched away before her time, like a torch brightly kindled and then in a little while letting fall its flame—still further, that the suffering reaches to you seems to me no less grievous. For least of all men did our noble Himerius deserve to come to the trial of anything painful, a man both excellent in eloquence and to us the most longed-for of friends. Yet, if it were another to whom I had to write of these things, I should surely need many words for this—that what has befallen is human, and that to bear it is necessary, and that nothing more is gained by grieving the more, and all that seemed fitting for the consolation of grief, as though teaching one who did not know. But since I count it shameful, toward a man who knows how to admonish others, to make those speeches by which one must school the ignorant to self-control, come, leaving the rest aside, I will tell you the tale—whether of a wise man, or rather a true account—not strange to you, perhaps, but unknown, as is likely, to most; using which alone, as a grief-assuaging drug, you may find release from your suffering not less than that of the cup which the Laconian woman is believed to have offered to Telemachus for an equal need. For they say that Democritus of Abdera, when Darius grieved for the death of a fair wife, and he had nothing to say that would suffice for consolation, promised him to bring her back to the light, if he were willing to furnish whatever was needed for the purpose. Darius bade him spare nothing, but take whatever he might and make good his promise; and Democritus, having paused a little while, said that everything for the doing of the deed was provided him, save one thing only, which he himself knew not how to get, but which Darius, as king of all Asia, would perhaps not find hard to discover. And when Darius asked what so great a thing it was that the king alone might know, Democritus, they say, answered and said: if he should inscribe upon the tomb of his wife the names of three men who had never mourned, she would straightway come to life again, being shamed by the law of the rite. And Darius being at a loss, and unable to find anyone to whom no grievous thing had ever befallen, Democritus, laughing as was his wont, said: "Why then, O strangest of men, do you mourn without measure, as though you alone were entangled in so great a grief, you who cannot find even one of all who have ever lived without his share of a private sorrow?" But these things Darius needed to hear, a barbarian and uneducated man, given over to pleasure and passion; but you, a Hellene and one who honours true education, ought to have the remedy from yourself, since otherwise it would be a shame to your reason, if it had not the same power as time.
To Dositheus

Your son Diogenes, having shown himself to me after your departure, and having said that you were angry with him, as a father might be vexed with a son, begged me to become a mediator of his reconciliation with you. If, then, his fault was moderate and such as you can bear, yield to nature, and, knowing that you are a father, return in your judgement toward your son; but if he has stumbled in something too great for pardon to reach, you yourself would be the juster judge, whether you ought, having borne even this nobly, to overcome your son's purpose by a better judgement, or whether you should entrust the trial of his fault to the chastening of a longer time.
To Plutarchus

To me even a small letter from you suffices to court the occasion of great pleasure. And so, being greatly pleased with what you wrote, I give back the like myself, judging that the friendships of comrades ought to be repaid not by the length of letters so much as by the greatness of goodwill.
To Eugenius

In all respects my body is moderately well, and besides, the affairs of my mind too go well. And I think there can be no better proem to a letter sent by friend to friend. Of what, then, is it the proem? Of a request, I think. And what is the request? Of letters in return; which I would they might agree in their thought also with mine, announcing the same favourable tidings from you to us.
To the governor of Greece (or to a curator)

I have given order that ships be built at Cenchreae. As to how many, the governor of the Hellenes will tell you; but as to how the care of the matter should be taken, hear it from us: free of all bribe-taking, and quickly. And that you may not repent of such a service, I myself, with the gods' help, will take thought.
To Libanius

We ought, indeed, obeying the Delphic precept, to know ourselves, and not dare to be over-confident in face of the hearing of so great a man, against whom even to look, when merely seen, is hard, much less to come to a level with him when he sets in motion his all-wise harmony; since, even if Pan should sound a clear melody, anyone might stand aside in awe, were he even Aristaeus, and at Apollo's playing upon the cithara anyone might be still, even if he knew the music of Orpheus. For the lesser ought justly to give way to the greater, so far as it is the lesser, if it is to know what is its own and what is not. But whoever has hoped to set a mortal melody against an inspired music has not learned, it seems, the fate of Marsyas the Phrygian, nor of the river named after him, which bears witness to the punishment of the maddened flute-player; nor has he heard of the death of Thamyris the Thracian, who set his voice against the Muses with no good fortune. Why need I speak of the Sirens, whose feathers still the victorious Muses bear upon their brows? But of those each, for his unmusical daring, even now pays a sufficient penalty in men's memory; whereas we ought, as I said, to stand within our own borders, and, while we drink our fill of your music, to be still, like those who receive in quiet the oracle of Apollo as it comes forth from the holy shrine. But since you yourself woo from us the keynote of the song, and, as it were with the wand of Hermes, with your own words you move and rouse us from sleep, come, just as those who, when Dionysus strikes his thyrsus, are borne, unloosed, to the dance, so too let us, under your plectrum, sound back what is fitting, like those who attend the leader of the chorus at the recall of the rhythm. And first let us begin for you with the discourse which lately, at the king's command, we wrought upon the famous bridging of the strait—since this is what seems good to you—giving small in return for great, and in truth bronze for gold, but feasting our own Hermes with such gifts of hospitality as we have. Surely not even Theseus disdained Hecale's plain supper, but knew how to be content with little for what was needful. And Pan, the god of shepherds, did not scorn to set the herdboy's pipe to his lips. Receive, then, the discourse with a gracious nod, and do not shrink from lending a great ear to a little song. But if it has anything skilful in it, the discourse itself is fortunate, and its maker has gained the witness of Athena's vote besides. But if it needs still a perfect hand for the filling-up of the whole, do not yourself disdain to add what is wanting. Surely the god, when called upon by an archer, has stood beside him and laid his hand to the dart, and to a lyre-singer chanting the high-pitched strain the Pythian, with the help of a cicada, sounded the like for the lacking string.
To Iamblichus (a fictitious composition transmitted in the corpus)

O Zeus, how is it well that we should pass our days in the heart of Thrace and winter in the silos there, while from the fair Iamblichus, as from some morning spring, letters are sent us instead of swallows, and yet it is permitted neither to us to come to him nor to him to come to us? Who would willingly accept this, unless he were some Thracian, a worthy match for Tereus? "Lord Zeus, but do you deliver from Thrace the Achaeans; make a clear sky, and grant our eyes at last to see" our own Hermes, and to greet his halls and to cling to his shrines, as they say Odysseus did when, after his wandering, he saw Ithaca. But him the Phaeacians set down still sleeping, like some piece of merchandise, out of the ship, and departed; whereas us not even sleep takes hold of, until it be granted us to see you, the great benefit of the world. And yet you jest that you have transported all the East—both me and my comrade Sopater—into Thrace; but for us, if I must speak the truth, so long as Iamblichus is not present, a Cimmerian fog dwells with us. And you ask one of two things: either that we come to you, or that you come to us. For us the one is at once to be prayed for and profitable, to return to you ourselves and to enjoy your good things; but the other is better than every prayer. But since for you at least it is impossible and unprofitable, do you stay at home and rejoice and keep the quiet that you have, while we will bear nobly whatever the god grants. For it is the part of good men, they say, both to keep good hope and to do what is needful, but to follow the necessities of fortune.
To Iamblichus (transmitted in the corpus)

I confess that I have paid a sufficient penalty for your absence, not only by the hardships that befell me during my travels, but, more than these, by this very thing, that I have been parted from you for so long a time, though I have met with many and various fortunes everywhere, so as to leave nothing untried. For though I have endured the tumults of wars, and the constraint of a siege, and the wandering of flight, and fears of every kind, and besides the extremities of winters and the dangers of sicknesses, and from upper Pannonia to the crossing of the Calchedonian strait countless and manifold misfortunes, I would say that nothing has happened to me so painful or so hard to bear as that I, having left in the East you, the common good of the Hellenes, have for so long a time not seen you; so that, if I should say that a mist and a great cloud lie about my eyes, do not wonder. For then will calm air, and the brightest light of the sun, and as it were the truest and fairest spring of life surround me, when I embrace you, the great glory of the world, and, like a true-born son to a good father, seen against all hope returning from some war or sea-storm, and having told all that I suffered and through what dangers I came, and being, as it were, moored upon a sacred anchor, may find at last a sufficient solace for my pains. For it consoles, naturally, and lightens misfortunes, when one, making known to others what he has suffered, divides the knowledge of his trouble in the fellowship of speech. Meanwhile, with such means as I have, I attend to you according to my power; for I will not cease, during the time of our separation, to tend you with the token of letters. And if I should receive the like from you in return, I shall relax a little, holding converse with your letters as with some saving symbol. Do you receive graciously what comes from us, and show yourself the more gracious in return; for whatever you signify of good or write to us, this is judged by us in place of the voice of Hermes the eloquent, or the hand of Asclepius.
To Iamblichus (transmitted in the corpus)

"You have come, you have done well"; for you have come, even in your absence, by what you write; and I longed for you, and you set my heart aflame, burning with desire. So neither do I deny the love-charm, nor do I leave you in anything; but I behold you as present to my soul, and am with you though absent, and nothing suffices to bring me to satiety. Yet you do not cease both doing good to the present, ever, and to the absent giving, by what you write, not gladness only but very life. When, for instance, someone reported to me lately that a comrade had come bringing letters from you, I chanced to be on the third day of a disorder of the stomach, and was somewhat sorely afflicted in body, so as not to be even free of fever; but when it was signified, as I said, that the bearer of the letters was at my doors, I, like a man not master of himself and possessed, leapt up and rushed out before what was needful could be brought. And when I had but taken the letter into my hands, I swear by the gods themselves and by the desire for you that has kindled in me, at once my pains fled, and the fever too left me straightway, as though abashed by some manifest presence of the saviour. And when I had broken the seal and read, what soul do you think I had then, or with how much pleasure was I filled, praising and justly loving the dearest of winds, as you say, the truly amorous, the minister of fair things, because he became to me the servant of your letters, having directed your letter to us like a winged thing with a fair and conducting breeze, through which it was granted me not only to be gladdened, learning the natural tidings of you, but also, sick as I was, to be saved by you? But as for the rest—how shall I tell what I felt at first toward the letter, or how sufficiently make known my love? How often did I run back from the middle to the beginning? How often was I afraid lest, having finished, I should unawares...? How often, as in some circle and round of revolution, did I draw the close of the conclusion back to the beginning, as in a musical song giving back to the end the melody that led to the beginning of the rhythm? Yes, and by Zeus, what followed these things—how often did I press the letter to my mouth, as mothers embrace their children; how often did I cling to it with my mouth as though kissing my own dearest beloved; how often did I greet and kiss the very superscription, which had been sealed by your hand as by a clear signet, and then set it upon my eyes, as one clinging to the traces of the letters as to the fingers of that sacred right hand! Hail, then, yourself to us many times, as the fair Sappho says, and not only as many times as the time during which we have been parted from one another, but hail always, and write and remember us as is fitting. For us no time shall fail in which we shall not, everywhere and on every occasion and in every discourse, hold you in memory. But if anywhere "Zeus should grant us to come to our native land," and if again we should come beneath that sacred hearth of yours, spare us no longer as a fugitive, but bind us, if it please you, to your own dearest seats, as one who has caught a deserter from the Muses, and then chasten us with such penalties as suffice. Surely not even unwillingly shall I undergo the sentence, but willingly indeed and rejoicing, as the provident and saving correction of a good father. And if you should be willing to trust me even with the judgement against myself, and grant me to carry out the sentence I wish, I would gladly fasten myself, my noble friend, to your little tunic, that I might in no way be parted from you, but be ever with you and everywhere borne about, like those whom the fables fashion as men of double nature. Unless that too the fables tell as in play, but hint at the special quality of friendship, showing, in the bond of fellowship, the kinship of soul that runs through both.
To Iamblichus (transmitted in the corpus)

I perceive the sweetness of your reproach, and how you do both things at once, both honouring by what you write and instructing by what you charge against me. For my part, if I were conscious to myself of having failed, even a little, in my duty toward you, I should certainly either, by alleging reasonable excuses, try to escape the reproach, or, having erred, should not refuse to ask pardon, since I know you are not otherwise unforgiving toward your own, if we have offended in any of the friendly duties toward you against our will. But as it is—for it was neither lawful that you should be overlooked, nor we negligent, that we might obtain what, ever seeking, we long for—come, let me defend myself to you as in a written charge, and show that I have neither overlooked any of the things I ought toward you, nor even dared to delay.
To Iamblichus (transmitted in the corpus)

For Odysseus it sufficed, when checking his son's notion concerning him, to say: "No god am I; why do you liken me to the immortals?" But I would say that I am not even among men at all, so long as I am not with Iamblichus. Yet I confess to be your lover, as he was the father of Telemachus. For even if someone should say I am unworthy, not even so will he take from me my longing; since I hear that of fair statues many have become lovers, who not only did no harm to the art of the maker, but, by their passion for them, added to the work a living pleasure. As for the men of old and wise, among whom you wish in play to enrol me, I would say I fall as far short of them as I believe you yourself share in those men's company. And yet you—not Pindar only, nor Democritus, nor Orpheus the most ancient, but the whole Hellenic world together, all that is remembered to have come to the summit of philosophy—you hold blended, as in a lyre, by the harmonious composition of varied notes, to the perfection of music. And as Argus the guardian of Io, the fables, having care of Zeus's darling, fence about on every side with the sleepless dartings of his eyes, so too the discourse lights you up, the true guardian of virtue, with ten thousand eyes of culture. Proteus the Egyptian, they say, changed himself into varied shapes, as if fearing lest he should unawares reveal to those who sought him how wise he was; but I, if Proteus was really wise and such as to know many things, as Homer says, praise his nature, but do not admire his judgement, because he did the work not of any lover of mankind, but of a deceiver, hiding himself, that he might not be useful to men. But you, my noble friend, who would not truly admire, that you are in no way less than the wise Proteus—nay rather greater—since, perfected to the summit of virtue, you do not grudge men your fair things, but, like pure Helios, lead the rays of unmixed wisdom upon all, not only being with the present as is fitting, but glorifying the absent, so far as you can, by what comes from you? You would thus surpass even the fair Orpheus in what you do; for he spent his own music upon the ears of wild beasts, whereas you, as though born for the salvation of the common race of men, emulating everywhere the hand of Asclepius, come upon all things with a learned and saving nod. So that to me it seems that Homer too, if he came to life again, would far more justly riddle in your case the verse: "And one still somewhere is kept back alive in the wide world." For in truth, of the old mint, a kind of sacred spark of true and fruitful culture is kindled in you alone. And may it be, O Zeus the saviour and Hermes the eloquent, that the common benefit of all the inhabited world, the fair Iamblichus, be preserved for the longest time. Surely, in the case of Homer and Plato and Socrates and any other worthy of that company, the granting of a just prayer, when it was the good fortune of those before, so increased their times to greater things. Nothing, then, hinders that in our day too a man worthy, both in word and in life, of those men, should, by like prayers, be escorted to the uttermost of old age, for the happiness of mankind.
To Serapion the elder (on figs and on the number one hundred)

Others keep festivals in various ways, but I send to you, as a token of a sweet feast, a pleasant gift, a hundred long-stemmed figs of our country, courting for you a pleasure small in the greatness of the gift, but, in its excellence, perhaps sufficient. Now Aristophanes thinks the fig, save for honey, sweeter than all other things, and does not even allow that to be sweeter than the fig, as he says, judging the matter himself; while to Herodotus the historian, for the showing of a true desolation, it sufficed to say: "Among whom there are neither figs nor any other good thing," as though no other good thing among fruits were of more account than figs, nor any good thing at all needed by those among whom the fig is found. And the wise Homer praises the other fruits for size or colour or beauty, but to the fig alone he grants the title of sweetness. And honey he calls "green," fearing lest unawares he should call sweet what often befalls to be bitter; but to the fig alone he renders its proper praise, as to nectar, since it alone of all is sweet. And honey, Hippocrates says, is sweet to the taste, but altogether bitter in the digestion; and I do not disbelieve the saying; for all agree that it is productive of bile and turns the humours to the contrary of the taste. And this the more accuses its nature of an inborn bitterness; for it would not change into what is bitter, unless this had altogether belonged to it from the beginning, from which it passed over to the other. But the fig is sweet not to the taste only, but is better also in the digestion. So beneficial is it to men that Aristotle says it is even an antidote against every deadly poison, and that for this reason at banquets it is set out before the other dishes and eaten after them as a relish, as though, in place of some sacred safeguard, it embraced the wrongs done by foods. And further, that the fig is dedicated to the gods, and is the offering laid on the altar at every sacrifice, and that it is better than all frankincense for the preparing of incense, this is no peculiar saying of mine, but whoever has learned its use knows that it is the saying of a wise man and hierophant. And the fair Theophrastus, in his precepts of husbandry, setting forth the generations of grafted trees, and what yield to graftings of one with another, praises, I think, above all plants, the tree of the fig, as being receptive of varied and diverse generation, and alone of the rest easily bearing the growth of every kind, if one, cutting off each of its branches, and then breaking it, should fit into the several stocks another sprouting growth, so that often the sight of it alone suffices in place of a whole garden, as though, in some most graceful meadow, it sent back from itself a varied and manifold splendour of fruits. And the other tree-fruits are short-lived and do not endure to be kept; but the fig alone may be carried over the year and meet the generation of the coming fruit; so that Homer too says that in the garden of Alcinous the fruits grow old upon one another. With the others, perhaps, this would seem a poetic fable; but with the fig alone it would agree with the plain truth, since it alone of the other fruits is more lasting. Such, I think, being the nature of the fig, far better is its growth among us, so that, while it is more precious than the other plants, that of our country is more wonderful than the fig elsewhere; and that, while it surpasses the others in its generation, it is itself, in turn, surpassed by ours, and again, by its inclusion under both heads, is preserved—like to the victor, while in the things in which it seems to be surpassed, again, on the whole, being the victor. And this not unreasonably befalls among us alone; for it was fitting, I think, that the city truly of Zeus, and the eye of all the East—I mean the sacred and greatest Damascus—which surpasses all other places in everything, in the beauty of her temples and the greatness of her shrines and the temperate blending of her seasons and the splendour of her springs and the multitude of her rivers and the fertility of her soil, should alone suffice, even with such a plant, for the surpassing of the marvel. For the tree endures no transplanting, nor passes beyond the bounds of its native growth, but, by the law of an indigenous plant, refuses generation from abroad. And gold, I think, and silver, the same, grow in many places; but our land alone bears a plant unable to grow elsewhere. And as the imports from the Indians, and the Persian silks, or whatever is born in the land of the Ethiopians—born and so reported—pass everywhere by the law of commerce, so too our fig, growing nowhere else of the earth, is sent everywhere by us, and there is neither city nor island which it does not visit with the marvel of its sweetness. Nay, it adorns even a royal table, and is a stately ornament of every feast; and neither cake, nor twist, nor any newly-baked bread, nor any other kind of seasoned dainty, is its equal wherever it comes; so great is its excellence over the other dishes and over the figs of every place. And the other figs either are eaten in their autumn season or, when dried, go into the storehouse; but ours alone serves both uses, and is fair upon the tree, but far fairer if it come to the drying. And if you should take in with the eye its beauty upon the trees, and how it hangs from each of the stocks by long stems, as it were after the manner of buds, or how the tree runs round in a circle with its fruit, one upon another in a row, forming a circular variegated splendour, you would say it contrives this as it were a necklace upon a throat. The plucking of them from the trees, too, and the contrivance for their long keeping, hold an ambition not less than the pleasure of their use; for they are not, like the other figs, thrown together all at once, nor dried in a heap or loosely in the sun, but first they are gently plucked from the trees by the hands, then hung upon the walls by twigs or thorny rods, that they may whiten as they come into contact with the pure sun, and remain unmolested by beasts and birds, guarded, as it were, by the protection of their thorns. And concerning their generation and sweetness and season and preparation and use, these things our letter plays out to you.
To Sapor, king of the Persians (a forgery, transmitted in the corpus)

Showing, as I have until now, my inborn calm and love of mankind from childhood, I have received as subjects all who dwell beneath the sun. For behold, every race of barbarians, even to the borders of the river Ocean, has come bearing gifts to my feet; and likewise the Sagadares, reared by the Danube, and the Goths of varied and shaven aspect, who have no appearance like to men but a savage form: these in the present time grovel at my footsteps, promising to do whatever befits my empire. And not in this alone am I drawn on, but I must with all speed overtake the land of the Persians and put to flight that Sapor, the descendant of Darius, until he become tributary and subject to me; and thence to lay waste the dwelling-places of the Indians and of the Saracens, until they too all become, in the second rank of my empire, tributary and subject. But you have thought beyond their power, alleging that you have clothed yourself in piety, while you put forward shamelessness, and everywhere proclaim that I have proved unworthy of the empire of the Romans. Or do you yourself not know that I am the descendant of the most mighty Constans? And though these things are thus known to us, on your account I have not departed from my former disposition, in which, while still young in years, I and you together shared. But with calm mind I decree that ten times a hundred pounds of gold be sent to me by you at my passage by Caesarea, while I am still upon the highway, being about with all speed to march upon the Persian war, ready, if you do not do this, to overturn every place of Caesarea, and to raze to the ground the fair-wrought monuments long since raised in it, and to set up temples and statues, that I may persuade all to yield to the king of the Romans and not be lifted up. The gold above named, therefore, having weighed and measured it out by number on the Campanian balance with security, send to me by some servant trusty to you, sealed with your own ring, so that, when I have recognised the inexorableness of the occasion, even though it be late, I may be made calm toward you concerning your offences. For what I have read, I have learned and condemned.
To Eustathius (a letter on piety, transmitted in the corpus)

The nearness of your land—I mean Ionia—has brought us very great gain. For when we were grieved and distressed at the first reports, it consoled us. What it is that I mean, you shall learn. It came to our ears that you had revolted from your former religion, handed down from your forefathers, and had driven on toward a vain superstition, lured to this by some evil counsellor of a gadfly. And what was I likely to suffer in my displeasure? For as, if I should learn that some good thing of yours was being proclaimed, I count it my own gain, so too any grievous thing—which I do not believe—I likewise reckon rather my own loss. Being grieved, then, at these things, the presence of our father Aetius gladdened me, announcing the contrary, things to be prayed for by us; for he said that you were earnest about houses of prayer, and were not far drawn away from the remembrance of those athletic men, and altogether he affirmed that you hold to the god-fearing ways of our own. And I would say to you, after the Homeric manner: "Strike thus," and by such remembrances gladden those who love you, remembering that there is nothing higher than reverence for the gods. For virtue at its summit teaches us to hate falsehood as deceitful, and to cling to the truth, which is shown most of all in the worship concerning the divine. For the multitude is altogether contentious and unstable; but that which alone, with one, is the minister and rules over the whole, not from a portioning-out and a lot, like the children of Cronos, but being its own beginning, and ruling over all, neither having received it by force from another, but being before all things—this is truly God, whom, with the worship that is owing, one ought to adore. Farewell.
To a friend (or to Libanius)

How profitable to us was the delay of the warrant! For instead of trembling and being afraid as I was borne along on the public carriage and fell in with drunken muleteers and with mules, "barley-fed," in Homer's phrase, through idleness and surfeit, and instead of enduring dust and strange cries and the cracking of whips, it has befallen me to journey at leisure, by a way overarched and shady, holding many springs and many resting-places suited to the season, in which to relieve my weariness; so that there appeared to me a halting-place, airy and ample, beneath certain plane-trees or cypresses, with the Phaedrus in my hands, or some other of the discourses of Plato. These things, then, dear friend, while I enjoy the freedom of my travel, I thought it strange not to share with you also and signify to you.
